skeleton.note: interrogative adverb 'how', this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: preposition 'toward', governs the dative, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: adversative conjunction, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: first-person plural pronoun, subject, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: preposition 'behind/after', governs the instrumental, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: formal/plural second-person pronoun, subject, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: preposition 'along', governs the dative, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: pronoun 'everything', accusative, this sentence's target word

takeaway.note: Тут is a more colloquial version of здесь — essentially the same meaning, different register.

skeleton.note: place adverb 'here', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: здесь is the basic adverb for 'here'.

grammarFocus.construction: здесь ('here,' standard adverb)

skeleton.note: interrogative adverb 'where', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: где asks about location.

skeleton.note: interrogative pronoun 'who', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: кто asks 'who' and grammatically always takes masculine singular agreement.

skeleton.note: determiner 'all/whole', masculine singular, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: весь is a universal determiner that inflects for gender/number/case — a different word from the pronoun всё.

grammarFocus.construction: весь + accusative (duration)

variations.note: Female speaker, past tense: работала.
Plural subject: работали.

Shifts from past tense to a statement of the state itself.

skeleton.note: reflexive possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: свой is the reflexive possessive, referring back to the subject itself.

grammarFocus.construction: Reflexive possessive свой

Using нравиться gives a more general 'I like' phrasing.

takeaway.note: A key determiner that refers back to the subject's own possession, regardless of the subject's person.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner, first-person plural, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: наш marks possession by a group including the speaker.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive наш (inanimate accusative = nominative)

variations.note: Female addressee, past tense: видела.
Formal/plural addressee: видели.

заметить ('to notice') is a close alternative.

paraphrases.simplest: Где наш столик? — most practical when looking for a seat.

takeaway.note: The plural-owner possessive — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: formal possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: ваш is the formal/plural 'your'.

grammarFocus.construction: Formal possessive ваш inside a quoted construction
grammarFocus.note: Ваш ('your,' formal) appears here inside direct quotation marks «...» — a polite phrase a staff member might say to a customer.

variations.note: Subject changed to third person (a different speaker).
Female speaker, past tense: сказала.

options.note: Drops ваш for a more concise confirmation.
Among friends, твой replaces the formal ваш.

paraphrases.simplest: Заказ готов? — the most concise phrasing in a casual setting.

takeaway.note: Essential in polite service contexts — note the твой/ваш distinction for casual vs. formal.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: мой is the first-person singular possessive, agreeing with its noun's gender/number/case.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive мой (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because телефон is inanimate, мой ('my') in the accusative matches its nominative form (мой телефон).

variations.note: Female addressee, past tense: нашла.
Formal/plural addressee: нашли.

options.note: Asks about location directly rather than whether it's been found.
Directly checks whether the other person has it.

paraphrases.simplest: Где мой телефон? — most practical when searching for a lost item.

takeaway.note: The most frequent possessive — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: informal possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: твой marks possession by someone you address informally.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive твой (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because подарок is inanimate, твой ('your,' informal) in the accusative matches its nominative form (твой подарок).

variations.note: Female addressee, past tense: нашла.
Formal/plural addressee: нашли / ваш подарок.

options.note: Asks about location directly.
The reflexive нашёлся ('turned up') gives a more spontaneous nuance.

paraphrases.simplest: Где твой подарок? — most practical when searching for a lost item.

takeaway.note: The informal possessive for someone close — switch to ваш for a formal addressee.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'his', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: его ('his') is an indeclinable possessive, identical in form to он's genitive.

replies.gloss: Yeah, I know it by heart.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive его
grammarFocus.note: Его ('his') never changes form regardless of the gender, number, or case of the noun it modifies — it's fixed, derived from the owner's own gender.

Formal/plural addressee: помните.

options.note: Asks directly 'what's his number?'
Shifts to asking whether you can reach him, rather than whether you remember the number.

paraphrases.simplest: Какой у него номер? — most practical when you just want the number itself.

takeaway.note: The key point: его, её, and их never change form no matter the gender, number, or case of the noun they modify.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'her', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: её ('her') is an indeclinable possessive determiner.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive её
grammarFocus.note: Её ('her') stays the same form regardless of the modified noun's gender, number, or case, just like его and их.

variations.note: Turned into a question.
Subject changed to plural.

options.note: The standard fixed phrase for 'what's her name?'
Using известный ('known') gives a more formal phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Как её зовут? — the most standard way to ask someone's name.

takeaway.note: An extremely common fixed phrase for asking 'what is his/her name?'

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'their', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: их ('their') is an indeclinable possessive determiner.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive их
grammarFocus.note: Их ('their') also stays the same form regardless of the modified noun's gender, number, or case, just like его and её.

variations.note: Formal/plural addressee: знаете.
Changed to third person.

options.note: A direct 'what's their last name?'
Using известный ('known') gives a more formal phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Как их фамилия? — the most standard, simple way to ask.

takeaway.note: Worth memorizing as a set: all three third-person possessives are invariant.

skeleton.note: reflexive pronoun, accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: себя is a reflexive pronoun with no nominative form — it always appears in an oblique case.

grammarFocus.construction: чувствовать себя + instrumental (state expression)
grammarFocus.note: Себя ('oneself,' reflexive accusative) is used in the fixed phrase чувствовать себя; the following state word (here an adverb, плохо) describes how one feels.

variations.note: Turned into a question.
Subject changed to plural.

options.note: A shorter impersonal way to say you feel unwell.
неважно ('not great') softens it a bit.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне плохо. — the shortest, most everyday way to say you feel unwell.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pattern for 'to feel (a certain way)' — себя itself never changes form.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: друг is a masculine noun with an irregular plural, друзья.

grammarFocus.construction: Zero-copula sentence with adjective agreement
grammarFocus.note: Мой ('my') and хороший ('good') both agree with друг (a masculine noun); быть is absent.

variations.note: For a female addressee: подруга, and хорошая agrees.
For multiple addressees: друзья, хорошие.

options.note: отличный ('excellent') gives a stronger compliment.
Using дружба ('friendship') evaluates the relationship itself.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты хороший друг. — dropping мой gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: In Russian, adjectives and possessives must always agree with the noun's gender, number, and case.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: the plural of человек is not человеки but the suppletive form люди.

grammarFocus.construction: человек (always grammatically masculine) + adjective agreement

variations.note: Still хороший человек even with a formal addressee.
Same form with a third-person subject.

options.note: 'You have a kind heart' — a more figurative compliment.
добрый ('kind') alone is a shorter compliment.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты хороший. — dropping человек gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: The key point: человек stays grammatically masculine even when describing a woman.

skeleton.note: demonstrative determiner, masculine accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: этот is a demonstrative determiner that inflects for gender/number/case, unlike the invariant pronoun это.

grammarFocus.construction: Demonstrative этот (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because столик is inanimate, этот ('this') in the accusative matches its nominative form (этот столик).

variations.note: Female addressee, past tense: выбрала.
Formal/plural addressee: выбрали.

options.note: нравиться ('to like') shifts toward the reason for the choice.
Using садиться ('to sit down') is a more action-oriented suggestion.

paraphrases.simplest: Садимся здесь? — most practical when deciding where to sit.

takeaway.note: The basic demonstrative for something nearby — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: demonstrative determiner, masculine accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: тот means "that (far)" and pairs with этот "this (near)".

grammarFocus.construction: Demonstrative тот (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because вечер is inanimate, тот ('that') in the accusative matches its nominative form (тот вечер).

variations.note: Changing the noun to день keeps the same structure.
Formal/plural addressee: помните.

options.note: тогда ('back then') avoids naming a specific noun.
Adds особенный ('special') to share the impression of that evening.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты помнишь тот вечер? — the simplest phrasing as is.

takeaway.note: The key distinction between something close by (этот) and something farther off or already mentioned (тот).

skeleton.note: pronoun "everything", accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: всё (everything) is an invariant pronoun, used here as the accusative direct object.

grammarFocus.construction: всё (neuter object pronoun)
grammarFocus.note: Всё ('everything') is a neuter pronoun referring to 'all things/matters,' functioning as the verb's accusative object.

variations.note: Turned into a question.
Subject changed to plural.

options.note: Using ясно ('clear') in an impersonal construction.
The perfective понял expresses 'have fully understood.'

paraphrases.simplest: Мне всё ясно. — a very natural way to express understanding.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pronoun for 'everything' — always stays neuter, never changes form.

skeleton.note: negative response particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: нет is the basic "no" response particle.

grammarFocus.construction: Negative response particle нет
grammarFocus.note: Нет ('no') negates the response as a whole, separate from the verb negation (не хочу) in the following clause.

variations.note: Subject changed to plural.
Changed to third-person feminine.

options.note: Dropping нет and answering with just the negated verb.
The fixed polite way to decline.

paraphrases.simplest: Нет, спасибо. — the most natural way to politely refuse.

takeaway.note: A two-layer negation pattern: нет to open the answer, then не before the verb within the sentence.

skeleton.note: affirmative response particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: да is the basic affirmative particle.

grammarFocus.construction: Affirmative response particle да
grammarFocus.note: Да ('yes') is the basic affirmative particle, with the following clause (я знаю) elaborating on it.

variations.note: Subject changed to plural.

Adding конечно ('of course') strengthens the certainty.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern of affirming, then adding supporting detail.

skeleton.note: мочь, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

grammarFocus.note: Мочь ('to be able') governs an infinitive (спать); negation goes right before мочь itself.

keyPoint: сказать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of speaking.

Changed to third person.

options.note: The fixed phrase иметь в виду ('to mean, intend').

paraphrases.simplest: Что ты имеешь в виду? — most natural when checking what someone means.

takeaway.note: An extremely common pattern for checking the intent behind someone's words.

skeleton.note: говорить, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: говорить is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act/ability of speaking.

grammarFocus.construction: говорить (imperfective) + adverb медленно

paraphrases.simplest: Я говорю медленно. — dropping очень gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: The most frequent modal construction for 'wanting to (do something).'

skeleton.note: хотеть, 3rd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: хотеть has irregular conjugation (singular stem хоч-, plural stem хот-).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + infinitive спать
grammarFocus.note: Хочет ('wants') is followed by the infinitive спать ('to sleep') — an extremely common pattern for expressing sleepiness.

skeleton.note: идти, 2nd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: идти is the imperfective unidirectional verb of motion.

keyPoint: делать is an imperfective verb of general "doing/making".

skeleton.note: видеть, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

skeleton.note: думать, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: думать takes о + prepositional case for "to think about".

skeleton.note: restrictive particle "only", this sentence's target word

keyPoint: только is a particle meaning "only".

keyPoint: ещё means "more/still" as an adverb.

options.note: можно ('may I') is a more polite way to request.
добавить ('to add') is another phrasing.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pattern for asking for a refill/more of something.

keyPoint: уже means "already", pairing with ещё не ("not yet").

вернуться ('to return,' perfective) is another option.

keyPoint: очень is the basic intensifying adverb "very".

grammarFocus.note: Очень ('very') modifies люблю ('love'), intensifying the emotion.

keyPoint: сейчас is a simple adverb meaning "now".

paraphrases.simplest: Я на работе. — very natural when briefly stating your situation.

takeaway.note: The basic adverb for emphasizing an action happening right now.

skeleton.note: adverb "now (as opposed to before)", this sentence's target word

keyPoint: теперь implies a change from how things were before, unlike plain сейчас.

keyPoint: потом is a temporal adverb meaning "later".

потом changed to сейчас ('now').

можем ('we can') makes it a more tentative suggestion.

paraphrases.simplest: Поговорим позже? — already quite natural without давай.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for 'let's (do something)' — equivalent to English 'let's.'

keyPoint: просто means "simply/just", and is also used colloquially as a filler for emphasis.

grammarFocus.construction: просто ('just, simply') + шутишь

variations.note: Formal/plural addressee: шутите.
Changed to third person.

options.note: да ('right?') carries a similar confirming nuance.
Using the noun шутка ('a joke') is shorter and more direct.

takeaway.note: A frequent adverb for downplaying or restricting the significance of something.

keyPoint: тоже is a colloquial adverb meaning "also/too".

paraphrases.simplest: Я согласен. — for plain agreement this one short-form adjective is simplest.

takeaway.pattern: готов / готова / готовы + infinitive (ready to do something)
takeaway.note: Frequent in negotiation. согласиться marks what you agree to with с + instrumental (a person) or на + accusative (terms).

keyPoint: доказать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of proving.

grammarFocus.construction: можешь (2nd person singular of мочь) + perfective infinitive (доказать) + accusative (это), marked as a question by intonation
grammarFocus.note: Russian questions keep the statement word order; intonation (and the question mark in writing) does the work.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses можете
adding an instrumental of means: 'prove it with facts'

options.note: using the noun доказательства ('evidence') with у + genitive
asking with the instrumental interrogative чем ('with what')

paraphrases.simplest: У тебя есть доказательства? — in conversation this is the most direct and natural way to ask.

takeaway.pattern: Questions keep statement word order and rely on intonation
takeaway.note: No auxiliary inversion as in English. If there is a question word, it goes first (Чем ты докажешь?).

skeleton.note: обещать, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: обещать was originally biaspectual; in modern usage пообещать serves as its perfective.

grammarFocus.construction: обещаю (present, 1st person singular) + dative (тебе) + infinitive (помочь)
grammarFocus.note: обещать takes the person promised in the dative and the content as an infinitive. помочь also governs the dative, so 'to help you' is помочь тебе.

variations.note: the dative вам for formal or plural address
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is обещаем

options.note: обязательно ('definitely') + perfective future, focused on the action
using the set phrase дать слово ('to give one's word')

paraphrases.simplest: Я помогу, обещаю. — perfective future plus обещаю is what people actually say.

takeaway.note: помогать/помочь also takes the dative (помочь тебе) — using the accusative for the person helped is a frequent mistake.

keyPoint: простить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of forgiving.

grammarFocus.construction: можешь (2nd person singular of мочь) + perfective infinitive (простить) + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: простить takes the person forgiven in the accusative (простить меня); to name the offence as well, use простить мне что (dative + accusative).

variations.note: formal or plural address uses можете

variations.ru: Ты можешь простить мне эту ошибку?
variations.note: dative + accusative: 'can you forgive me this mistake?'

options.note: apologising directly with the imperative
using извинить, a lighter apology

paraphrases.simplest: Прости меня. — when apologising, the imperative is the simplest and most natural.

takeaway.note: Three registers to keep straight: Прости (casual), Простите (polite), Извини(те) (light).

keyPoint: вспомнить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of recalling.

grammarFocus.construction: могу (1st person singular of мочь) + perfective infinitive (вспомнить) + accusative (имя, an irregular -мя neuter noun) with не
grammarFocus.note: имя inserts -ен- from the genitive onward, but its accusative is identical to the nominative: имя.

variations.ru: Я не могу вспомнить его имя.
variations.note: adding a possessive: 'his name'
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is можем

options.note: using забыть ('to forget'), more direct
an idiom: 'the name flew out of my head'

paraphrases.simplest: Я забыл имя. — shortest and perfectly clear in conversation.

takeaway.pattern: вспомнить (to recall) / помнить (to remember) / забыть (to forget)
takeaway.note: вспомнить is the perfective moment of recall; помнить is the imperfective state of remembering. Learn all three together.

skeleton.note: past masculine, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: заметить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of noticing.

replies.gloss: I was here the whole time.

grammarFocus.construction: заметил (perfective past, masculine singular) + accusative (тебя) with the negation не
grammarFocus.note: заметить is the perfective of noticing something at a moment. The object stays accusative even under negation here (a genitive object is also possible).

variations.note: a female speaker uses не заметила
with a 1st-person plural subject, не заметили

options.note: using видеть ('to see'), more general
with an apology — what people actually say

paraphrases.simplest: Я тебя не видел. — simplest way to say you didn't notice someone.

takeaway.note: замечать/заметить is noticing something that comes into view — distinct from понять ('to understand') and узнать ('to find out').

keyPoint: узнать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of finding out.

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (узнать) + accusative (правду, feminine -у)
grammarFocus.note: узнать is the perfective 'to find out, to learn.' The feminine правда takes the accusative правду.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is хотим
adding всю (feminine accusative) for emphasis

options.note: the imperfective знать makes it a state: 'I want to know'
using the imperative of рассказать, more direct

paraphrases.simplest: Я хочу знать правду. — the version people use most often in conversation.

takeaway.pattern: узнать (to find out, perfective) / знать (to know, imperfective)
takeaway.note: узнать is learning something new; знать is holding the knowledge. New information vs. standing state.

keyPoint: предложить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of proposing.

grammarFocus.construction: можно (impersonal predicate) + perfective infinitive (предложить) + accusative (план)
grammarFocus.note: можно takes no subject and is followed by an infinitive to ask 'may I…?' — the standard way to request permission.

variations.note: adding the dative мне to name who is asking
with a different object: 'may I suggest a different plan?'

options.note: using the imperative of разрешить, noticeably more formal
using the noun предложение to open without asking permission

paraphrases.simplest: Можно предложить? — dropping the object makes it light enough for any meeting.

takeaway.note: The core permission pattern. Learn it with Можно мне…? and its negative counterpart Нельзя + infinitive.

skeleton.note: предлагать, 2nd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: предлагать is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act of proposing.

grammarFocus.construction: the interrogative pronoun что (accusative) + предлагаешь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: The inanimate interrogative что is identical in the nominative and accusative; here it is the verb's object, placed first.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses предлагаете
the perfective future asks what you will propose, as a single act

options.note: using the noun предложения ('suggestions')
'what shall we do?' — more colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Что предлагаешь? — dropping ты is the most natural version in speech.

takeaway.pattern: Put the interrogative что (nominative = accusative) first
takeaway.note: Unlike animate кто (accusative/genitive кого), что shows no case distinction — the verb's government tells you which case it is.

skeleton.note: полагать, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: полагать is a stative imperfective verb meaning "to suppose".

grammarFocus.construction: полагаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + the adverb так
grammarFocus.note: полагать is a stative verb meaning 'to suppose,' rather formal in register; так полагаю is the set way to say 'I suppose so.'

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is полагаем
adding a что clause to state the content of the supposition

options.note: using думать — the most common, colloquial choice
using казаться + dative for a more tentative 'it seems so to me'

paraphrases.simplest: Я так думаю. — the simplest, most natural version in everyday speech.

takeaway.pattern: Я полагаю, что... / Я думаю, что... / Мне кажется, что...
takeaway.note: Three registers for stating an opinion: полагать is bookish, думать neutral, кажется the most tentative.

keyPoint: представить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of imagining/presenting.

grammarFocus.construction: можешь (2nd person singular of мочь) + perfective infinitive (представить) + accusative (это)
grammarFocus.note: In the sense 'to imagine,' представить often adds the reflexive dative себе — представить себе — though speech usually drops it.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses можете
the fuller version with себе (same meaning)

options.note: a single imperfective word meaning 'can you imagine? / you won't believe it' — very common in speech
using вообразить ('to picture'), slightly bookish

paraphrases.simplest: Представляешь? — one word is the simplest and most natural way to share surprise.

takeaway.note: Beyond the literal 'imagine,' it works as a conversational opener meaning 'listen to this.'

skeleton.note: представлять, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: представлять is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act of representing/introducing.

grammarFocus.construction: представляю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + accusative (нашу компанию — feminine, -ую/-ию)
grammarFocus.note: In the sense 'to represent,' представлять is imperfective and stative. A feminine noun phrase in the accusative pairs -ую with -ию (компания → компанию).

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is представляем
with a masculine noun (inanimate, so accusative = nominative)

options.note: из + genitive is the most common way to state where you're from
using работать в + prepositional

paraphrases.simplest: Я из этой компании. — shortest and most natural when introducing yourself.

takeaway.note: The standard business introduction. Careful: the perfective представить means 'to introduce' or 'to present,' a different sense.

skeleton.note: существовать, 3rd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: существовать is imperfective, expressing the ongoing state of existing.

grammarFocus.construction: существует (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) with the nominative subject такой человек, marked as a question by intonation
grammarFocus.note: существовать is a stative imperfective ('to exist'). The demonstrative такой agrees in gender and number (такой/такая/такое/такие).

variations.note: with a feminine noun it becomes такая
in the plural both adjective and verb go plural

options.note: using бывать ('to happen to exist'), more colloquial
разве ('surely not') + есть adds a note of disbelief

paraphrases.simplest: Такие люди бывают? — in speech бывать sounds more natural here.

takeaway.pattern: такой / такая / такое / такие ('such a…', agreeing in gender and number)
takeaway.note: такой always agrees with its noun, and it is also the standard exclamation word: Такой красивый!

skeleton.note: past masculine, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: исчезнуть is perfective, denoting a single completed act of vanishing.

grammarFocus.construction: исчез (perfective past, masculine singular) + the adverb вдруг
grammarFocus.note: Most verbs in -нуть drop the -ну- in the past (исчезнуть → исчез, исчезла) — and the masculine form takes no -л at all.

variations.note: with a feminine subject, исчезла (the -л- reappears outside the masculine)
in the plural, исчезли

options.note: using пропасть ('to go missing'), more colloquial
не стало + genitive — 'he was suddenly gone,' also a euphemism for dying

paraphrases.simplest: Он вдруг пропал. — пропасть is what people actually say.

takeaway.pattern: The past tense of -нуть verbs (исчез / исчезла / исчезли)
takeaway.note: Same group as привыкнуть → привык and погибнуть → погиб: no -л in the masculine past.

skeleton.note: past masculine, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: появиться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of appearing.

grammarFocus.construction: появился (reflexive perfective past, masculine singular) + the adverb вдруг
grammarFocus.note: появиться is reflexive; the -ся stays in the past: появился / появилась / появились.

variations.note: with a feminine subject, появилась
in the plural, появились

options.note: using прийти ('to come'), more concrete
an idiom: 'he sprang up as if out of the ground'

paraphrases.simplest: Он вдруг пришёл. — when a person shows up, прийти is the natural verb.

takeaway.note: Learn the pair together. появляться is 'to keep appearing'; появиться is a single appearance.

keyPoint: подойти is perfective, denoting a single completed act of approaching.

grammarFocus.construction: подойди (perfective imperative) + ко + dative (мне)
grammarFocus.note: The preposition к becomes ко before awkward consonant clusters: ко мне, ко всем.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses подойдите
a different к + dative target (к stays as к)

options.note: идти + сюда ('come here') — the most colloquial option
adding пожалуйста to soften it

paraphrases.simplest: Иди сюда. — shortest and most natural with someone close to you.

takeaway.pattern: к + dative ('toward, over to') / ко мне (a phonetic variant)
takeaway.note: The к/ко choice is purely about pronunciation — memorise ко мне, ко всем, ко вторнику as units.

skeleton.note: подходить, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: подходить is imperfective, expressing the state of "suiting/fitting".

grammarFocus.construction: подхожу (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + dative (тебе)
grammarFocus.note: In the sense 'to suit, to be right for,' подходить takes the dative. In the physical sense 'to walk up to,' it takes к + dative.

variations.note: the dative вам for formal or plural address
with a thing as subject: 'does this job suit you?'

options.note: нравиться + dative turns it into a question about liking
adding как + nominative to name the role

paraphrases.simplest: Я тебе подхожу? — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: подходить + dative ('to suit, to be right for')
takeaway.note: Это мне подходит ('that works for me') is essential for arranging plans. Physical approach is подходить к + dative.

keyPoint: зайти is perfective, denoting a single completed act of dropping by.

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (зайти) + в + accusative (магазин)
grammarFocus.note: зайти is to drop in somewhere along the way; the destination takes в/на + accusative. The perfective infinitive makes it a single errand.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is хотим
к + dative makes it 'drop in on a friend'

options.note: надо + в + accusative with no verb at all — very common in speech
using заглянуть ('to pop in'), lighter

paraphrases.simplest: Мне надо в магазин. — dropping the verb makes it the shortest option.

takeaway.pattern: зайти в + accusative (into a place) / зайти к + dative (to a person)
takeaway.note: Places take в/на + accusative, people к + dative — the heart of how motion verbs work.

keyPoint: снять is perfective, denoting a single completed act of taking off [clothing].

grammarFocus.construction: можно (impersonal predicate) + perfective infinitive (снять) + accusative (пальто, an indeclinable neuter noun)
grammarFocus.note: пальто never changes form, so the accusative looks the same. снять is to take off something you're wearing.

variations.note: adding the dative мне to name who is asking
with a normally declining feminine noun the accusative is куртку

options.note: using мочь, slightly more direct
asking where to leave it — practical in someone's home

paraphrases.simplest: Можно снять пальто? — the natural set phrase when arriving somewhere.

takeaway.pattern: снять (to take off) ↔ надеть (to put on)
takeaway.note: Learn снять пальто and надеть пальто together. снять also means 'to rent' and 'to film' — a busy word.

keyPoint: снимать (here "to film/photograph") is imperfective, expressing an ongoing act.

grammarFocus.construction: нельзя (impersonal predicate of prohibition) + imperfective infinitive (снимать) + the adverb здесь
grammarFocus.note: нельзя with an imperfective infinitive means 'it is forbidden'; with a perfective infinitive it means 'it is impossible.'

variations.note: with фотографировать ('to photograph')
with a different prohibited activity

options.note: a noun plus the short passive participle запрещена — the wording you see on signs
a negative imperative (imperfective) stopping someone directly

paraphrases.simplest: Здесь нельзя снимать. — simplest for saying it out loud.

takeaway.note: Compare Здесь нельзя парковаться ('no parking') with Его нельзя найти ('he can't be found').

keyPoint: сесть is perfective, denoting a single completed act of sitting down.

grammarFocus.construction: можно (impersonal predicate) + perfective infinitive (сесть) + the adverb здесь
grammarFocus.note: сесть is the perfective 'to sit down' (the act), while сидеть is 'to be sitting' (the state). Asking about a seat calls for сесть.

variations.note: adding the dative мне to name who is asking
with рядом ('next to you')

options.note: 'is this seat free?' — by far the most common thing people actually say
asking from the other side, with занято ('taken')

paraphrases.simplest: Здесь свободно? — in a café or on a train this is overwhelmingly the natural question.

takeaway.pattern: сесть (to sit down, perfective) / сидеть (to be sitting, imperfective)
takeaway.note: Садитесь, пожалуйста ('do have a seat') is the polite imperfective imperative; Сядьте sounds like an order.

keyPoint: встать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of getting up.

grammarFocus.construction: the short-form adjective должен (obligation) + perfective infinitive (встать) + the adverb сейчас
grammarFocus.note: должен agrees with the subject (должен/должна/должны). встать is the perfective 'to get up, to stand up.'

variations.note: a female speaker uses должна
in the plural, должны

options.note: dative + нужно + infinitive, softer
пора ('it's time to') + imperfective infinitive

paraphrases.simplest: Мне пора вставать. — the natural thing to say in the morning.

takeaway.pattern: должен + infinitive (must) / пора + infinitive (it's time to)
takeaway.note: должен expresses obligation, пора the right moment — and пора normally takes an imperfective infinitive.

keyPoint: вставать is imperfective, expressing habitual getting up.

grammarFocus.construction: dative (мне) + the impersonal predicate трудно + imperfective infinitive (вставать) + the time adverb утром
grammarFocus.note: Impersonal predicates like трудно, легко and приятно take no subject; the person experiencing it goes in the dative. The habit calls for the imperfective вставать.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person masculine experiencer (dative ему)
with легко ('easy') instead

options.note: using с трудом ('with difficulty') plus a conjugated verb
using любить + infinitive to frame it as a preference

paraphrases.simplest: Мне трудно вставать утром. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: The core impersonal pattern — the same frame as Мне холодно ('I'm cold') and Мне интересно ('I find it interesting').

keyPoint: бросить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of throwing.

grammarFocus.construction: брось (perfective imperative) + dative (мне) + accusative plural (ключи — inanimate, accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: брось ends in a soft sign. The inanimate plural ключи is identical in the accusative and nominative.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses бросьте
with a masculine singular object

options.note: using кинуть ('to chuck'), more colloquial
using передать ('to pass') if you'd rather it not be thrown

paraphrases.simplest: Кинь ключи. — shortest and most colloquial among friends.

takeaway.note: бросить also means 'to quit' — бросить курить ('to quit smoking'). Context changes everything.

keyPoint: поймать (here "to catch/hail a taxi") is perfective, denoting a single completed act.

replies.gloss: Let's book one through an app.

grammarFocus.construction: помоги (perfective imperative) + dative (мне) + perfective infinitive (поймать) + accusative (такси, indeclinable)
grammarFocus.note: помочь takes the person helped in the dative. такси never changes form, and поймать такси is the set phrase for hailing a cab.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses помогите
a different dative: 'help her'

options.note: using вызвать ('to call, to order') — the phrasing for a phone or app
turning it into a question about where to find one

paraphrases.simplest: Вызови такси, пожалуйста. — with ride apps the norm, вызвать is the practical choice.

takeaway.note: помочь is one of the key dative verbs. Also keep поймать такси (to hail) apart from вызвать такси (to order).

keyPoint: стрелять is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act of shooting.

replies.gloss: I don't want to hurt you.

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative: не + imperfective imperative (стреляй) + в + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: Negative commands take the imperfective. стрелять marks the target with в + accusative (стрелять в цель).

variations.note: formal or plural address uses не стреляйте
with a different в + accusative target

options.note: не надо + infinitive — 'there's no need to shoot'
a concrete instruction: 'lower your weapon'

paraphrases.simplest: Не стреляй! — dropping в меня is shortest and most urgent.

takeaway.note: The target takes в + accusative, the weapon из + genitive (стрелять из пистолета) — note how the prepositions divide the work.

skeleton.note: защищать, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: защищать is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act of protecting.

replies.gloss: What are you protecting them from?

grammarFocus.construction: защищаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + accusative (свою семью) with the reflexive possessive свой
grammarFocus.note: свой means 'belonging to the subject,' and works with any person — Я защищаю свою семью. The feminine accusative is свою.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person subject свою means his own family (его would suggest someone else's)
with a plural accusative: свои права

options.note: using заботиться о + prepositional ('to take care of')
using стоять за + accusative ('to stand by')

paraphrases.simplest: Я защищаю свою семью. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: свой (the subject's own) vs его / её (someone else's)
takeaway.note: Он любит свою жену ('his own wife') and Он любит его жену ('someone else's wife') differ completely. свой is essential grammar.

keyPoint: защитить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of protecting.

replies.ru: Спасибо, я чувствую себя в безопасности.
Я могу сам о себе позаботиться.
replies.gloss: I can take care of myself.

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (защитить) + accusative (тебя)
grammarFocus.note: The perfective защитить is result-oriented — to get you protected; the imperfective защищать is ongoing defence.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is хотим
with the formal or plural accusative вас

options.note: the negated оставить — 'I won't abandon you'
'I'll be right here' — warmer and more natural

paraphrases.simplest: Я буду рядом. — in real conversation this carries more weight and sounds more natural.

takeaway.pattern: защищать (ongoing defence) / защитить (to get someone protected)
takeaway.note: Aspect separates sustained protection from a single rescue, and хочу + perfective is result-oriented.

keyPoint: победить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of winning.

grammarFocus.construction: the short-form adjective должны (obligation, plural) + perfective infinitive (победить)
grammarFocus.note: победить is defective: it has no 1st person singular future. 'I will win' has to be Я одержу победу or Я смогу победить.

variations.note: with a masculine singular subject, должен
addressing a woman, должна

options.note: using выиграть ('to win' a game or a prize)
using the noun победа with dative + нужна

paraphrases.simplest: Мы должны выиграть. — in sports выиграть is the more usual verb.

takeaway.pattern: победить has no 1st person singular future (a defective verb)
takeaway.note: There is no *я побежду. Use Я смогу победить or Я одержу победу instead.

keyPoint: спасти is perfective, denoting a single completed act of saving/rescuing.

replies.ru: Да, что бы это ни стоило.

grammarFocus.construction: хочешь (2nd person singular of хотеть) + accusative (меня, placed before the verb) + perfective infinitive (спасти)
grammarFocus.note: Russian word order is flexible, and pronoun objects usually sit before the verb: Ты хочешь меня спасти?

variations.note: formal or plural address uses хотите
the object after the infinitive — same meaning, slightly different emphasis

options.note: помочь + dative — gentler and more realistic
жалко + dative + accusative — 'do you feel sorry for me?'

paraphrases.simplest: Ты хочешь мне помочь? — the natural choice in an ordinary situation.

takeaway.pattern: Pronoun objects naturally go before the verb
takeaway.note: Я тебя люблю, Он меня не понимает — pronouns before the verb, while noun objects normally follow it.

skeleton.note: болеть, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: болеть is imperfective, expressing the ongoing state of being/getting sick.

grammarFocus.construction: болею (imperfective present, 1st person singular, in the sense 'to be ill') + the frequency adverb редко
grammarFocus.note: болеть has two patterns: for a person being ill it conjugates болею, болеешь; for an aching body part only the 3rd person болит / болят is used.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person singular subject (болеет)
with a different frequency adverb and a season

options.note: using почти не ('hardly ever')
using the noun здоровье ('health') with у + genitive

paraphrases.simplest: Я редко болею. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: болеть ('a person is ill': болею) / болеть ('a body part aches': болит)

options.note: using в + prepositional — by far the most common phrasing
using войти в + accusative to describe the action of going in

paraphrases.simplest: Она уже в кафе. — в + prepositional is overwhelmingly more natural in speech.

takeaway.note: Use внутри when the interior itself matters; everyday 'being inside' is just в + prepositional.

keyPoint: рядом is an adverb fossilized from the instrumental of ряд ("row").

grammarFocus.construction: сидит (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + рядом с + instrumental (со мной, with the phonetic со)
grammarFocus.note: рядом с governs the instrumental. The preposition с becomes со before мной for ease of pronunciation (со мной, со всеми).

variations.note: with a 2nd-person instrumental (с тобой keeps plain с)
with a plural subject (сидят)

options.note: using около + genitive ('next to'), which changes the case
using вместе and making both people the subject

paraphrases.simplest: Она сидит рядом. — dropping со мной still reads clearly from context.

takeaway.pattern: рядом с + instrumental ('next to') / около + genitive ('near')
takeaway.note: Memorise со мной / с тобой / с ним as units — со appears purely for pronunciation (со мной, со всеми, со стола).

keyPoint: вокруг means "around".

grammarFocus.construction: смотрю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + the adverb вокруг (which as a preposition takes the genitive)
grammarFocus.note: With no object вокруг is an adverb ('around'); with a noun it becomes a preposition governing the genitive — вокруг дома ('around the house').

variations.note: adding the genitive of себя to say 'around myself'
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is смотрим

options.note: the single reflexive verb оглядываться ('to look around')
осматриваться ('to take in one's surroundings'), more deliberate

paraphrases.simplest: Я смотрю вокруг. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: вокруг as adverb / вокруг + genitive as preposition
takeaway.note: Many words do double duty this way (внутри, около, после) — and they always take the genitive when a noun follows.

keyPoint: наверное is a hedging adverb meaning "probably".

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical наверное (commas on both sides) + zero copula + the adverb дома
grammarFocus.note: Words of supposition or evaluation — наверное, возможно, конечно — are set off by commas. дома means 'at home' and needs no preposition.

variations.note: with a feminine subject (the predicate doesn't change)
with a plural subject

options.note: using думать with a clause to express the guess
using скорее всего ('most likely'), a shade more certain

paraphrases.simplest: Он, наверное, дома. — the natural, compact way to guess.

takeaway.note: Also keep дома ('at home') apart from домой ('homeward') — both are adverbs and take no preposition.

keyPoint: возможно is a hedging adverb meaning "possibly".

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical возможно (set off by commas) + perfective future (придёт) + the adverb завтра
grammarFocus.note: возможно marks a low degree of certainty. The perfective future придёт presents the arrival as a single completed event.

variations.note: with a masculine subject (придёт is unchanged)
with a plural subject the verb is придут

options.note: using the colloquial может быть ('maybe')
не исключено, что ('it's not out of the question that'), formal

paraphrases.simplest: Может быть, она придёт завтра. — может быть is what people say in conversation.

takeaway.pattern: Degrees of certainty (точно > наверное > возможно / может быть)
takeaway.note: Pick by how sure you are. возможно and может быть are near-synonyms, the latter more colloquial.

keyPoint: точно means "exactly" and is also used to add emphasis, "really/for sure".

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb точно + не + знаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) — a case where word order changes the meaning
grammarFocus.note: точно не знаю means 'I don't know for sure'; не знаю точно means 'I don't know exactly.' The position of точно changes what the negation covers.

variations.ru: Я точно не знаю, когда он придёт.
variations.note: adding a когда clause to say what you don't know
with a 1st-person plural subject, не знаем

options.note: using the negated short-form adjective уверен ('sure')
a set colloquial phrase: 'I haven't the faintest idea'

paraphrases.simplest: Я не знаю. — dropping точно is simplest.

takeaway.pattern: точно не знаю ('I don't know for sure')
takeaway.note: точно means both 'exactly' and 'definitely' — in Он точно придёт it's emphatic certainty.

keyPoint: особенно is an emphatic adverb meaning "especially".

grammarFocus.construction: любить + accusative (кофе, an indeclinable masculine noun) + the added phrase особенно + the time adverb утром
grammarFocus.note: особенно emphasises whatever follows it; to say 'especially in the morning,' keep особенно утром together after the comma.

variations.note: with a different drink and time
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is любим

options.ru: Я больше всего люблю кофе утром.
options.note: using больше всего ('most of all')
using the adjective утренний with a dash construction for emphasis

paraphrases.simplest: Я люблю кофе, особенно утром. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: It goes immediately before what it emphasises, so its position determines the meaning.

keyPoint: обычно is a frequency adverb meaning "usually".

replies.gloss: Do you drink it in the evening too?

grammarFocus.construction: the frequency adverb обычно + пью (irregular 1st person singular of пить) + accusative (кофе) + the time adverb утром
grammarFocus.note: Frequency adverbs like обычно pair with the imperfective to express habit; they cannot go with a perfective.

variations.note: with a different drink
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is пьём

options.note: по + dative plural ('every morning') strengthens the habit
using каждое утро ('every morning,' accusative)

paraphrases.simplest: Я обычно пью кофе утром. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: Frequency adverbs (обычно / часто / редко / иногда) + imperfective
takeaway.note: Habits are always imperfective. Pair them with по утрам and по выходным (по + dative plural).

keyPoint: быстро means "quickly".

grammarFocus.construction: the intensifier очень + the adverb of manner быстро + говоришь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: очень modifies adverbs as well as adjectives (очень быстро). When adverbs stack, the intensifier comes first.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses говорите
слишком ('too') turns it into a complaint

options.note: the comparative медленнее in an imperative — a request instead
using успевать за + instrumental ('I can't keep up')

paraphrases.simplest: Говори медленнее, пожалуйста. — if you're actually struggling, this request is the useful one.

takeaway.note: очень is neutral emphasis; слишком implies it has gone too far.

keyPoint: тихо means "quietly".

grammarFocus.construction: imperfective imperative (говори) + the adverb тихо + a coordinate reason clause (все спят)
grammarFocus.note: The imperfective imperative asks for a sustained manner. спят is the 3rd plural of спать (сплю, спишь… спят).

variations.note: formal or plural address uses говорите
with the comparative тише ('more quietly')

options.note: dropping the verb entirely — the most practical version
the negated imperative of шуметь ('don't make noise')

paraphrases.simplest: Тише! — one word does the whole job.

takeaway.pattern: Imperfective imperative (sustained manner) / perfective imperative (one act)
takeaway.note: Говори тихо ('keep your voice down') vs Скажи ('say it once'). One-word comparatives like Тише! are everywhere.

keyPoint: легко means "easily".

replies.gloss: She has a good sense of humor.

grammarFocus.construction: the reflexive verb смеётся (imperfective present, 3rd person singular of смеяться) + the adverb легко
grammarFocus.note: смеяться always carries -ся. What you laugh at is marked with над + instrumental (смеяться над шуткой).

variations.note: with a masculine subject (the verb form is unchanged)
with a plural subject the verb is смеются

options.note: using часто ('often') to frame it as frequency
using рассмешить + accusative ('she's easy to make laugh')

paraphrases.simplest: Она часто смеётся. — more natural for 'she laughs a lot.'

takeaway.note: Not the accusative — над + instrumental is the rule. смеяться над собой ('to laugh at oneself') is common.

skeleton.note: impersonal predicate, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: трудно is an impersonal predicate taking a dative.

grammarFocus.construction: dative (мне) + the impersonal predicate трудно + perfective infinitive (понять) + accusative (это)
grammarFocus.note: трудно takes the dative. The perfective infinitive понять frames the difficulty as reaching understanding at all; the imperfective понимать would frame the process as difficult.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person masculine experiencer (dative ему)
with легко ('easy') instead

options.note: the negated мочь + infinitive — more direct
an idiom: 'that's beyond my understanding'

paraphrases.simplest: Я не понимаю. — shortest if that's all you need to say.

takeaway.pattern: dative + трудно / легко + infinitive (hard / easy to do)
takeaway.note: A perfective infinitive makes the achievement hard; an imperfective one makes the process hard. Aspect carries the meaning.

keyPoint: серьёзно is the adverbial form of серьёзный ("serious").

grammarFocus.construction: говорю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + the adverb серьёзно (from the adjective серьёзный via -о)
grammarFocus.note: Russian adverbs are normally formed by replacing the adjective ending with -о: серьёзный → серьёзно, быстрый → быстро.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is говорим
adding the accusative это: 'I mean this seriously'

options.note: the negated шутить ('I'm not joking') — the most colloquial option
using the short-form adjective серьёзен as predicate

paraphrases.simplest: Я не шучу. — the version that really lands when you need to be taken seriously.

takeaway.note: This is how adverbs are built — and note it coincides with the impersonal predicate form (Мне трудно).

keyPoint: правильно means "correctly".

grammarFocus.construction: говоришь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular) + the adverb of manner правильно, placed after the verb
grammarFocus.note: Adverbs of manner can sit before or after the verb; at the end of the sentence the adverb becomes the point being evaluated.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses говорите
the adverb before the verb (slightly less emphatic)

options.note: the short-form adjective прав ('right') — the shortest option
using согласен с + instrumental ('I agree with you')

paraphrases.simplest: Ты прав. — the shortest and most natural way to agree (Ты права to a woman).

takeaway.note: The short-form adjective прав agrees in gender and number — the most frequent way to signal agreement.

keyPoint: ясно means "clearly".

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb ясно + accusative (всё) + объясняет (imperfective present, 3rd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: всё ('everything') behaves as a neuter singular pronoun, identical in the accusative and nominative. ясно is an adverb of manner.

variations.note: with a masculine subject
the perfective past gives the result: she explained it all

options.note: using хорошо ('well') — the more common compliment
using становиться понятно ('things become clear with her')

paraphrases.simplest: Она хорошо объясняет. — the most natural form of this compliment.

takeaway.note: It pairs with predicates constantly: Всё понятно ('it's all clear'), Всё хорошо ('everything's fine').

keyPoint: эй is an attention-getting interjection.

grammarFocus.construction: the interjection эй + a zero-copula question (ты здесь?)
grammarFocus.note: эй is a casual 'hey.' With no present-tense verb for 'to be,' ты здесь? on its own asks whether someone is there.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses вы
есть + кто-нибудь: 'is anyone there?'

options.note: with тут, the colloquial equivalent of здесь
on a call or online: алло + слышать ('can you hear me?')

paraphrases.simplest: Ты здесь? — dropping эй is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: эй (a casual hail) / ты здесь? (zero-copula presence check)
takeaway.note: эй is quite informal — not for elders or superiors. здесь and тут are synonyms, тут more colloquial.

keyPoint: из-за is a preposition requiring the genitive, meaning "because of".

grammarFocus.construction: reflexive perfective past (расстроилась) + из-за + genitive (дождя)
grammarFocus.note: из-за marks an unwelcome cause and always takes the genitive; for a welcome cause use благодаря + dative.

variations.note: with a masculine subject (расстроился)
with a genitive plural cause

options.note: using the transitive расстроить + accusative, making the cause the subject
using переживать to describe an ongoing state of worry

paraphrases.simplest: Она расстроилась из-за дождя. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: из-за + genitive (a bad cause) / благодаря + dative (a good one)
takeaway.note: из-за дождя ('because of the rain') vs благодаря тебе ('thanks to you') — different cases, so learn them as a pair.

skeleton.note: indefinite pronoun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: что-нибудь means "anything/something".

grammarFocus.construction: хочешь (2nd person singular of хотеть) + accusative (что-нибудь, an indefinite pronoun)
grammarFocus.note: что-нибудь means 'something, anything at all.' Only the что part declines; -нибудь never changes (чего-нибудь, чему-нибудь).

variations.note: formal or plural address uses хотите
the genitive чего-нибудь with an infinitive: 'want something to drink?'

options.note: using dative + нужно
the future of быть — the most colloquial 'want anything?'

paraphrases.simplest: Будешь что-нибудь? — the natural way to offer food or drink.

takeaway.pattern: что-нибудь (anything at all) / что-то (something specific but unknown)
takeaway.note: Offers take что-нибудь; 'something happened' takes что-то. -нибудь is indefinite, -то is definite but unidentified.

keyPoint: тем is an instrumental form of тот, used idiomatically to mean "precisely because of that".

grammarFocus.construction: the instrumental тем (from тот) + the emphatic particle и + the short-form adjective хороша
grammarFocus.note: тем и хороша is an idiomatic instrumental: 'that is exactly what's good about her.' The short form хороша agrees with the feminine subject as predicate.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the short form is хорош
with a plural subject, хороши

options.note: using именно этим ('precisely in this') to spell it out
using the noun достоинство ('merit')

paraphrases.simplest: Этим она и хороша. — swapping тем for этим makes the sense easier to follow.

takeaway.pattern: тем и хорош / хороша / хороши ('that's exactly what's good about…')
takeaway.note: An instrumental of respect ('in that regard'), and a neat place to see short-form adjective agreement.

skeleton.note: emphatic particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: ж is a colloquial shortening of же.

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech (colon plus guillemets) + the particle ж (short for же) + the 1st person plural hortative пойдём
grammarFocus.note: Russian direct speech is enclosed in «». ж is the colloquial clipping of же, and Что ж means 'well then.'

variations.note: with the full form же (same meaning, a touch more formal)
with пойдёмте for a formal or plural invitation

options.note: with ну что ('so, then?'), more colloquial
recast as indirect speech with предложить + infinitive

paraphrases.simplest: Она говорит: «Пойдём?» — dropping Что ж is shortest.

takeaway.note: The perfective 1st plural is the key hortative: пойдём, сделаем, посмотрим. Add -те for politeness: пойдёмте.

skeleton.note: indefinite pronoun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: кое-что means "something" (known to the speaker but left unnamed).

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (меня) + есть + the indefinite pronoun кое-что
grammarFocus.note: кое-что means 'a little something' the speaker has in mind. The prefix кое- stays put while что declines (кое-чего, кое-чему).

variations.ru: У меня есть кое-что для тебя.
variations.note: adding для + genitive: 'something for you'
with the neuter adjective интересное following the pronoun

options.ru: У меня есть что-то для тебя.
options.note: with что-то, suggesting the speaker hasn't pinned it down either
using показать + dative to state the intention

paraphrases.simplest: У меня есть кое-что. — ideal for building a little suspense.

takeaway.pattern: кое-что (something the speaker knows but won't name)
takeaway.note: Learn the trio: что-то (unknown to the speaker too), что-нибудь (anything at all), кое-что (known but unnamed).

skeleton.note: indefinite pronoun, genitive=accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: кто-нибудь means "anyone/someone".

grammarFocus.construction: знает (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + accusative (кого-нибудь — animate, so accusative = genitive)
grammarFocus.note: The accusative of кто-нибудь is кого-нибудь: as an animate pronoun, its accusative matches the genitive. -нибудь never changes.

variations.note: with a masculine subject
кого-то means she knows someone specific but unidentified

options.note: using the noun знакомые ('acquaintances') with у + genitive
reordered to put the location first

paraphrases.simplest: У неё здесь есть знакомые? — the way this is usually asked in conversation.

takeaway.note: кто-pronouns are animate, so accusative = genitive; что-pronouns are inanimate, so accusative = nominative.

keyPoint: уверить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of reassuring/convincing.

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + accusative (тебя) + perfective infinitive (уверить)
grammarFocus.note: уверить is 'to assure, to convince.' What you're assuring someone of takes в + prepositional (уверить в своей правоте). Pronoun objects naturally sit before the verb.

variations.note: with the formal or plural accusative вас

variations.ru: Я хочу тебя уверить в этом.
variations.note: adding в + prepositional to name what you're assuring them of

options.note: the imperfective 1st person уверяю ('I assure you') — far more common in speech
the imperative of поверить + dative — the most colloquial option

paraphrases.simplest: Поверь мне. — two words that actually reassure someone.

takeaway.note: Уверяю вас is the formal set phrase; day to day people say Поверь мне or Честное слово.

keyPoint: всё равно is a fixed idiom meaning "anyway / regardless".

grammarFocus.construction: the idiom всё равно ('all the same, anyway') + perfective future (придёт)
grammarFocus.note: всё равно literally means 'it's all the same'; as an adverbial it means 'anyway, regardless.' With a dative it becomes Мне всё равно ('I don't care').

variations.note: with a masculine subject
with a dative it shifts to 'I don't mind either way'

options.note: using так или иначе ('one way or another')
using в любом случае ('in any case')

paraphrases.simplest: Она всё равно придёт. — already the simplest and most natural.

takeaway.pattern: всё равно ('anyway' / with a dative, 'I don't care')
takeaway.note: Mid-sentence it means 'will do it regardless'; with a dative it means the person has no preference.

skeleton.note: indeclinable noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: мисс is an indeclinable title borrowed from English "Miss".

grammarFocus.construction: the perfective imperative простите (polite) + the indeclinable borrowed address мисс
grammarFocus.note: Простите is the standard polite 'excuse me' (Прости is the casual form). мисс is borrowed from English and never declines.

variations.note: with a male form of address (сэр is also indeclinable)
with Извините, a lighter apology or hail

options.note: with пожалуйста — the safest way to get someone's attention
in Russian, Девушка! is the usual way to address a young woman

paraphrases.simplest: Извините! — one word is the practical way to hail someone.

takeaway.pattern: Простите / Извините ('excuse me') + a form of address
takeaway.note: мисс and сэр are barely used in Russia; the norms are Девушка! for a young woman and Молодой человек! for a young man.

keyPoint: нормально means "normally/fine".

grammarFocus.construction: чувствовать себя (a fixed phrase with the reflexive себя) + the adverb нормально
grammarFocus.note: 'To feel a certain way' is чувствовать себя + an adverb — an adverb, not an adjective (нормально, хорошо, плохо).

variations.note: with a masculine subject (себя is invariable)
with плохо ('unwell')

options.note: using с + instrumental with всё нормально
using dative + the comparative лучше ('she's better now')

paraphrases.simplest: С ней всё нормально. — the natural way to say someone's fine.

takeaway.pattern: чувствовать себя + adverb (to feel a certain way)
takeaway.note: Как ты себя чувствуешь? ('how are you feeling?') is the phrase to know. себя can go before or after the verb.

keyPoint: волноваться is a reflexive verb meaning "to worry".

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative: не + reflexive imperfective imperative (волнуйся) + за + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: волноваться ('to worry') marks whom you worry about with за + accusative. Being a negative command, it takes the imperfective — не волнуйся.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses не волнуйтесь
with a different за + accusative

options.note: with переживать ('to fret'), equally colloquial
reassuring by stating the reason: 'I'll be fine'

paraphrases.simplest: Не волнуйся. — dropping за меня is shortest and very common.

takeaway.pattern: волноваться за + accusative (about a person) / о + prepositional (about a matter)
takeaway.note: Не волнуйся! is the standard reassurance. Keep it distinct from the transitive волновать ('to worry someone').

skeleton.note: indeclinable noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: миссис is an indeclinable title borrowed from English "Mrs."

grammarFocus.construction: the greeting Здравствуйте + the indeclinable borrowed address миссис
grammarFocus.note: Здравствуйте is a frozen imperative of здравствовать ('to be in good health'). миссис is borrowed from English Mrs. and never declines.

variations.note: with a male form of address (мистер is also indeclinable)
with someone close, the singular здравствуй

options.note: a time-of-day greeting, easy to use even with strangers
dropping the title — Russians normally use no honorific here

paraphrases.simplest: Здравствуйте! — Russian doesn't normally add titles like миссис.

takeaway.note: Three registers of greeting. миссис and мистер are barely used in Russian except when referring to foreigners.

skeleton.note: neuter noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: свидание is a regular hard-stem neuter noun.

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (меня) + nominative (свидание) — an есть-less construction for plans
grammarFocus.note: Dropping есть makes it 'I have a date (coming up).' свидание is an -ие neuter noun, with the prepositional свидании.

variations.note: adding сегодня to pin down the plan
with a 3rd-person plural subject

options.note: using идти на + accusative ('I'm off on a date')
using встречаться to state the actual arrangement

paraphrases.simplest: У меня свидание. — the shortest way to say what you have on.

takeaway.pattern: У меня + nominative ('I have X on')
takeaway.note: The same frame as У меня встреча, У меня экзамен, У меня свидание — with есть dropped.

keyPoint: здорово is colloquial for "great/awesome".

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + zero copula + the adverbial predicate здорово (an exclamation)
grammarFocus.note: здорово literally means 'healthily,' but colloquially Это здорово! is the predicate for 'that's great.'

variations.note: with круто ('cool'), more youth-slang
adding как ('how') to heighten the exclamation

options.note: with отлично ('excellent'), more neutral
using быть в восторге ('to be delighted') to describe the state

paraphrases.simplest: Здорово! — one word carries the whole exclamation.

takeaway.note: Отлично (formal-ish) → Здорово (neutral colloquial) → Круто (slang), in increasing informality.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: чувак is youth slang for "dude".

grammarFocus.construction: the casual greeting Привет + a nominative form of address (чувак, slang)
grammarFocus.note: Russian has no separate vocative case — you address people in the nominative. чувак is male slang, roughly 'dude.'

variations.note: with a female form of address
addressing a group (ребята — 'guys, everyone')

options.note: with друг ('friend'), gentler
with Здорово ('hey'), a casual male-to-male greeting

paraphrases.simplest: Привет! — dropping the address is safest and most natural.

takeaway.pattern: Forms of address use the nominative (Russian has no vocative)
takeaway.note: чувак is for close male friends only — never with strangers or at work.

keyPoint: вечером is a fixed adverb from the instrumental of вечер.

grammarFocus.construction: увидимся (perfective future, 1st person plural) + the instrumental-derived time adverb вечером
grammarFocus.note: The perfective future 1st plural doubles as the standard parting formula. The reflexive -ся carries the reciprocal 'each other.'

variations.note: with a different time
with позже ('later'), leaving the time open

options.note: до + genitive — the most compact parting phrase
with встретиться, which sounds more like a firm arrangement

paraphrases.simplest: До вечера! — two words, the natural way to part.

takeaway.note: До свидания, До вечера, До завтра, До встречи — all до + genitive, the backbone of Russian goodbyes.

keyPoint: вообще-то is a colloquial discourse marker that softens a correction.

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical вообще-то (set off by a comma) + a negated imperfective present
grammarFocus.note: вообще-то softens or corrects what was said — 'actually, as a matter of fact.' It usually opens the sentence, followed by a comma.

variations.note: with a different predicate: 'actually, I disagree'
with the parenthetical mid-sentence, commas on both sides

options.note: with честно говоря ('to be honest')
with если честно ('honestly'), more colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Честно говоря, не знаю. — the easiest opener to reach for.

takeaway.note: Both soften what follows, and both are set off by commas in writing.

keyPoint: увидеться is perfective, denoting a single completed instance of "seeing each other".

grammarFocus.construction: the short-form adjective должны (obligation, plural) + a reciprocal reflexive perfective infinitive (увидеться)
grammarFocus.note: The -ся in увидеться is reciprocal — 'see each other.' должны agrees with the plural subject мы.

variations.note: with встретиться, which implies a firmer arrangement
with dative + нужно + infinitive, gentler

options.note: надо бы, with the conditional particle бы, softens it to 'we really should'
давай + perfective 1st plural turns it into an invitation

paraphrases.simplest: Давай увидимся. — the natural, compact way to propose meeting.

takeaway.note: With a plural subject these mean 'do it to each other' — целоваться ('to kiss each other') works the same way.

keyPoint: ночью is a fixed adverb from the instrumental of ночь.

grammarFocus.construction: работает (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + the instrumental-derived time adverb ночью (ночь → ночью)
grammarFocus.note: Instrumentals of time take no preposition. The feminine -ь noun ночь gives ночью, used adverbially for 'at night.'

variations.note: with a different time (днём — 'in the daytime')
with a plural subject (работают)

options.note: using the noun смена ('shift') with в + accusative
using у + genitive with the adjective ночная работа

paraphrases.simplest: Он работает ночью. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: Instrumental time adverbs (утром / днём / вечером / ночью)
takeaway.note: Four parts of the day in the instrumental. Keep them apart from the iterative по утрам ('every morning').

keyPoint: утром is a fixed adverb from the instrumental of утро.

replies.gloss: Okay, see you in the morning.

grammarFocus.construction: увидимся (perfective future, 1st person plural) + утром (утро → утром, a neuter instrumental)
grammarFocus.note: утром is the instrumental of the neuter утро, used adverbially for 'in the morning.' Note the ending differs from feminine ночью (-ом vs -ью).

variations.note: with a different time (день → днём)
with a clock time it becomes утра (genitive)

options.note: до + genitive as a parting phrase
with встретиться instead

paraphrases.simplest: До утра! — the shortest way to sign off.

takeaway.pattern: утром ('in the morning,' instrumental) / в семь утра ('at seven am,' genitive)
takeaway.note: The same word takes the instrumental as an adverb but the genitive with a clock time — a core point of time expressions.

keyPoint: здравствуйте is a formal greeting.

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech (colon plus guillemets) + the greeting Здравствуйте, a frozen verb form
grammarFocus.note: Здравствуйте is the imperative of здравствовать, frozen as a greeting — grammatically the plural/polite imperative.

variations.note: with the familiar singular здравствуй
with a time-of-day greeting

options.note: using поздороваться ('to say hello') to report it indirectly
with a morning greeting

paraphrases.simplest: Она поздоровалась. — the most compact way to report it.

takeaway.note: To talk about greeting itself, use здороваться / поздороваться, with с + instrumental for the person greeted.

keyPoint: скорее is the comparative adverb meaning "sooner/faster".

grammarFocus.construction: the imperfective imperative иди + the comparative adverb скорее (from скоро)
grammarFocus.note: скорее is the comparative of скоро ('soon, quickly'), so it means 'faster.' Added to a command, it hurries someone along. The imperative of идти is иди.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses идите
with быстрее ('faster'), stressing physical speed

options.note: a single word to hurry someone — the shortest form
adding давай ('come on') to push colloquially

paraphrases.simplest: Быстрее! — one word says it all.

takeaway.note: Adverbial comparatives end in -ее or -е, and adding one to a command turns it into 'do it more so.'

keyPoint: ох expresses surprise or pain.

grammarFocus.construction: the interjection Ох + the perfective imperative прости + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: Ох expresses pain, regret or dismay and is set off by a comma. простить takes the person forgiven in the accusative.

variations.note: formal or plural apology uses простите
with Ой ('oops'), a lighter surprise

options.note: using извинить with пожалуйста — a lighter apology
using dative + жаль ('I'm so sorry')

paraphrases.simplest: Прости. — one word is enough to apologise.

takeaway.note: Ох is a sigh or regret, Ой a small start or twinge, Ах an exclamation. All sit at the front, set off by a comma.

skeleton.note: neuter noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: дерьмо is a vulgar word meaning "crap/garbage".

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + zero copula + a noun predicate (дерьмо, neuter, vulgar)
grammarFocus.note: Это + a noun is the zero-copula way to pass judgement. дерьмо is outright crude, so its use must be sharply limited.

variations.note: with ерунда ('nonsense'), far milder
with the adverbial predicate ужасно ('awful'), perfectly safe

options.note: indirect speech with плохо ('bad'), neutral
using the negated понравиться + dative, polite

paraphrases.simplest: Это плохо. — the neutral version to use in public or in class.

takeaway.note: дерьмо is vulgar; know the safe substitutes Это плохо, Это ужасно and Это ерунда.

keyPoint: беспокоиться is a reflexive verb meaning "to worry".

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative: не + reflexive imperfective imperative (беспокойся) + обо + prepositional (мне)
grammarFocus.note: о becomes обо before мне for pronunciation (обо мне, обо всём). беспокоиться marks what you worry about with о + prepositional.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses не беспокойтесь
with a different prepositional (о нём keeps plain о)

options.note: with волноваться за + accusative, which changes the case
reassuring by explaining: 'I'll be fine'

paraphrases.simplest: Не беспокойся. — dropping обо мне is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: обо мне / обо всём (a phonetic variant)
takeaway.note: о becomes обо before мне, всём and многом; о тебе and о нём keep plain о — memorise them as units.

keyPoint: алло is used specifically to answer the phone.

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + Алло, the interjection reserved for the telephone, with rising question intonation
grammarFocus.note: Алло is used only when answering a call or checking the line — never to hail someone face to face.

variations.note: with Да, слушаю ('yes, speaking'), more businesslike
following up with слышать to check the line

options.note: using снять трубку ('to pick up') with just Да?
using ответить на + accusative ('to answer the call')

paraphrases.simplest: Алло? — one word is all a phone call needs.

takeaway.note: In person use Эй or Простите — the restriction to phone calls is the point.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: детектив means both "detective" and "detective novel".

replies.gloss: What case are you working on?

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + a noun predicate (детектив, nominative — how professions are stated)
grammarFocus.note: No verb for 'to be' in the present, and no articles either, so the profession simply stands in the nominative: two words make a sentence.

variations.note: with a different profession, same shape
in the past был appears and the predicate goes instrumental: детективом

options.note: using работать + instrumental ('I work as a detective')
a dash construction: 'my profession is detective'

paraphrases.simplest: Я детектив. — the shortest way to state your job.

takeaway.pattern: Nominative predicate in the present (Я детектив) / instrumental in the past (Я был детективом)
takeaway.note: Once a linking verb appears, the predicate switches to the instrumental — the core of Russian predicate syntax.

keyPoint: немой means "mute".

grammarFocus.construction: the provoking insert ты что (set off by a comma) + the long-form adjective predicate немой
grammarFocus.note: Ты что…? expresses surprise or irritation — 'what, are you…?' немой can stand as a predicate in its long form.

variations.note: with a different adjective (глухой — 'deaf')
formal or plural (немые)

options.note: using молчать — calm and inoffensive
using слышать, which doesn't accuse the other person

paraphrases.simplest: Почему ты молчишь? — the version to use if you don't want to insult anyone.

takeaway.pattern: Ты что, …? ('what, are you…?' — provoking colloquial)
takeaway.note: Calling someone немой can be genuinely insulting; in real conversation it's best avoided.

keyPoint: заткнуться is a very colloquial perfective verb meaning "to shut up".

grammarFocus.construction: the reflexive perfective imperative Заткнись, standing alone as a crude command
grammarFocus.note: заткнуться literally means 'to plug oneself up.' The -нись ending is the singular imperative of a reflexive verb.

variations.note: formal or plural — still extremely rude
with замолчать — forceful, but less crude than заткнись

options.note: using помолчать with пожалуйста, much gentler
using тише ('quieter') — the politest option

paraphrases.simplest: Тише, пожалуйста. — the version to actually use.

takeaway.note: Four levels of 'be quiet.' Заткнись belongs to fights or close-friend joking, nowhere else.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: шутить is imperfective, expressing the act of joking.

grammarFocus.construction: шутишь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular) with question intonation — the set expression of disbelief
grammarFocus.note: An imperfective present question conveys 'you're joking, right?' The word order stays put; intonation does the work.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses шутите
adding да? to press for confirmation

options.note: one word for 'really?' — the most colloquial option
a set phrase for 'no way!'

paraphrases.simplest: Серьёзно? — one word conveys the surprise.

takeaway.pattern: Ты шутишь? / Серьёзно? / Да ладно! ('you're kidding')
takeaway.note: Three set reactions of surprise. Да ладно! is the most casual, for people you know well.

skeleton.note: indefinite adverb, this sentence's target word
