keyPoint: когда-нибудь means "someday".

grammarFocus.construction: увидимся (perfective future, 1st person plural) + the indefinite adverb когда-нибудь
grammarFocus.note: когда-нибудь means 'sometime' with the time left open. Don't confuse it with когда-то, which means 'once, at some point in the past.'

variations.note: with как-нибудь ('sometime, somehow')
adding может to lower the certainty further

options.note: with как-нибудь, even vaguer
adding надеюсь ('I hope') for warmth

paraphrases.simplest: Ещё увидимся! — the warmest brief way to close.

takeaway.note: -нибудь points to an indefinite future, -то to a definite past. They're easily confused — learn them as a pair.

keyPoint: погодить is a related word meaning "to wait a bit".

grammarFocus.construction: the perfective imperative Погоди + the quantity adverb немного
grammarFocus.note: погодить is a colloquial perfective meaning 'to hold on,' used almost exclusively in the imperative Погоди / Погодите. немного means 'a little.'

variations.note: formal or plural address uses погодите
with подождать — the more standard verb

options.note: with пожалуйста — the standard polite request
a set phrase: 'just a moment'

paraphrases.simplest: Одну минуту. — the natural phrase when you need someone to wait.

takeaway.note: Three ways to ask someone to wait. Погоди is for people you know; Подождите is the safe choice.

keyPoint: украсть is perfective, also used figuratively for "to steal [a kiss]".

grammarFocus.construction: хотите (formal or plural of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (украсть) + accusative (поцелуй — masculine inanimate, accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: украсть literally means 'to steal'; украсть поцелуй is a figurative 'to steal a kiss.' The person stolen from takes у + genitive.

variations.note: with someone close it becomes ты хочешь

variations.ru: Вы хотите украсть у меня поцелуй?
variations.note: adding у + genitive: 'steal a kiss from me'

options.note: using поцеловать + accusative, stated directly
using можно + infinitive to ask permission — the courteous option

paraphrases.simplest: Можно вас поцеловать? — asking permission is the appropriate form here.

takeaway.pattern: украсть + accusative + у + genitive ('to steal X from Y')
takeaway.note: Whom you steal from takes у + genitive (украли у меня телефон). The figurative украсть поцелуй is literary.

keyPoint: ужасно is colloquially used as an intensifier meaning "very".

grammarFocus.construction: the intensifier ужасно + устала (perfective past, feminine singular of устать)
grammarFocus.note: ужасно literally means 'awfully,' but colloquially it is just an intensifier. устать is perfective: reaching the state of being tired.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is устал
with a plural subject, устали

options.note: with очень ('very'), more neutral
using без + genitive ('she's worn out'), idiomatic

paraphrases.simplest: Она очень устала. — очень is the safe neutral intensifier.

takeaway.note: Originally negative, these work as pure intensifiers in speech — even positively, as in ужасно рад ('terribly glad').

skeleton.note: feminine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: задница is a vulgar word for "butt".

grammarFocus.construction: болит (3rd person singular) + у + genitive (меня) — the pain construction, here with the crude noun задница
grammarFocus.note: The construction itself is identical to У меня болит голова. задница is vulgar; medical contexts use ягодицы.

variations.note: with a neutral body part instead
with a 3rd-person masculine sufferer

options.note: using the euphemism ниже спины ('lower back area')
using больно + dative + infinitive ('it hurts to sit') to convey it from the situation

paraphrases.simplest: Мне больно сидеть. — polite enough for a doctor's office.

takeaway.pattern: У + genitive + болит + body part, plus a choice of register
takeaway.note: The grammar stays the same while the vocabulary changes the impression — in public, avoid задница and use a euphemism.

keyPoint: как-то means "somehow/vaguely".

grammarFocus.construction: the indefinite adverb как-то + the adverb of manner странно + улыбается (imperfective present, 3rd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: как-то means 'somehow, sort of' and hedges the statement; как-то странно reads as 'in some odd way.'

variations.note: with a masculine subject
with a different adverb (грустно — 'sadly')

options.note: using the noun улыбка with у + genitive
using как-то не так ('somehow not right'), more colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Она странно улыбается. — dropping как-то is shorter and more definite.

takeaway.note: как-то неудобно ('somehow awkward'), как-то грустно ('somehow sad') — a very common way to soften an impression.

skeleton.note: neuter noun, genitive, the target word

keyPoint: "Прошу прощения" is a fixed apology expression meaning "excuse me / I'm sorry."

grammarFocus.construction: прошу (imperfective present, 1st person singular of просить) + genitive (прощения) — the set apology
grammarFocus.note: просить takes what you ask for in the genitive (просить прощения, просить помощи). The subject я is normally dropped in this formula.

variations.note: adding за + accusative for what you're apologising for
просим when an organisation apologises

options.note: the most common, lighter apology
dative + жаль to express regret

paraphrases.simplest: Извините. — the natural choice for an everyday apology.

takeaway.note: просить takes the genitive for what is requested. Прошу прощения is more formal than Извините and fits a serious apology.

keyPoint: Сбежать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "running away."

replies.gloss: Where does he want to run off to?

grammarFocus.construction: хочет (3rd person singular of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (сбежать)
grammarFocus.note: сбежать is с- plus бежать, 'to run off.' Where from takes из + genitive, whom from takes от + genitive.

variations.note: with a plural subject (хотят)
adding из + genitive for where he wants to escape from

options.note: using уехать ('to leave'), neutral and milder
using мечтать + infinitive with бросить всё ('to drop everything')

paraphrases.simplest: Он хочет уехать. — the neutral way to put it.

takeaway.pattern: сбежать из + genitive (from a place) / от + genitive (from a person)
takeaway.note: The prefix с- means 'off, away from a surface.' сбежать с уроков ('to skip class') is a frequent extension.

keyPoint: Босс is a colloquial masculine noun for "boss."

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the possessive мой + a noun predicate (босс, nominative)
grammarFocus.note: No linking verb in the present, and мой agrees with the masculine босс, so it stays мой. Three words make the sentence.

variations.note: with a female boss it becomes моя начальница
in the past был appears and the predicate goes instrumental: моим боссом

options.note: with начальник ('boss'), the more standard word
using под руководством + genitive ('under his direction'), more formal

paraphrases.simplest: Он мой начальник. — босс is colloquial; начальник is safer in formal settings.

takeaway.pattern: Nominative predicate in the present, instrumental in the past (Он был моим боссом)
takeaway.note: A linking verb pushes the predicate into the instrumental. босс is a colloquial loanword; начальник is standard.

keyPoint: Круто here (colloquial for "cool/awesome") is the adverbial form of the adjective крутой.

grammarFocus.construction: считать + accusative (это) + an adverbial predicate (круто) — the 'consider X to be Y' frame
grammarFocus.note: считать ('to consider') takes accusative + instrumental (считает это глупостью) or, colloquially, accusative + adverb (считает это круто).

variations.note: with a masculine subject
with an instrumental adjective — the more standard construction

options.note: using нравиться + dative — the most natural option
using по мнению + genitive ('in her view')

paraphrases.simplest: Ей это нравится. — what people actually say.

takeaway.pattern: считать + accusative + instrumental / adverb ('to consider X to be Y')
takeaway.note: считать его умным is the standard instrumental pattern; an adverb instead is a colloquial judgement.

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Скучать is an imperfective verb that takes the construction по + dative.

grammarFocus.construction: скучаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + по + dative (тебе)
grammarFocus.note: In the sense 'to miss someone,' скучать takes по + dative — not the accusative or genitive. Learn скучаю по тебе and по дому as units.

variations.note: the dative вам for formal or plural address
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is скучаем

options.note: dative + не хватает + genitive ('I lack you'), more poetic
using ждать + genitive to look forward instead

paraphrases.simplest: Я скучаю по тебе. — the natural, idiomatic way to say it.

takeaway.note: скучать по дому ('to be homesick'), скучать по старым временам ('to miss the old days'). The по + dative pairing is obligatory.

keyPoint: Врать is an imperfective colloquial verb meaning "to lie."

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative: не + imperfective imperative (ври) + dative (мне)
grammarFocus.note: врать is a colloquial verb taking the person lied to in the dative. Negative commands take the imperfective. It conjugates вру, врёшь, with ё in the stem.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses не врите
with лгать ('to lie'), more bookish

options.note: the positive version: 'tell me the truth'
with обманывать + accusative, which changes the case

paraphrases.simplest: Говори правду. — the positive version accuses the other person less.

takeaway.pattern: врать + dative (to lie to someone) / обманывать + accusative (to deceive someone)
takeaway.note: врать (colloquial) and лгать (bookish) both take the dative; обманывать takes the accusative.

keyPoint: Осторожен is the short form of осторожный, used in predicate position.

grammarFocus.construction: the imperative of быть — будь — plus the short-form adjective осторожен as predicate
grammarFocus.note: The imperative of быть is будь (singular) / будьте (plural). The short form осторожен agrees in gender and number: осторожен / осторожна / осторожны.

variations.note: addressing a woman: осторожна
formal or plural: будьте осторожны

options.note: a one-word adverbial warning — the shortest form
using беречь себя ('take care of yourself'), a warm parting line

paraphrases.simplest: Осторожно! — for an urgent warning, one word does it.

takeaway.note: Many set phrases follow it: Будь добр ('be so kind'), Будьте здоровы ('stay well'). Don't forget the agreement.

keyPoint: Идиот is an insulting slang term.

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + a noun predicate (идиот, an insult)
grammarFocus.note: Ты + noun is the shortest possible sentence type, though идиот is a strong insult. The construction itself is the same as Ты студент.

variations.note: the feminine идиотка when addressing a woman
the plural идиоты

options.note: using the short-form adjective неправ ('wrong'), far cooler-headed
criticising the act rather than the person

paraphrases.simplest: Это было глупо. — criticising the action works better in practice.

takeaway.note: The frame is neutral; the word isn't. Learn the construction, skip the insult.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Минутка is a diminutive/affectionate form of минута.

grammarFocus.construction: попросила (perfective past, feminine singular) + accusative (минутку, a feminine noun with the diminutive -ка)
grammarFocus.note: минутка is the affectionate diminutive of минута, softening the tone. Its accusative is минутку.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is попросил
the plain, non-diminutive form

options.note: using the infinitive подождать ('to wait')
quoting the set phrase in direct speech

paraphrases.simplest: Она попросила минутку. — already the most natural version.

takeaway.note: Одну минутку and Секундочку are the everyday ways to say 'just a moment' — the diminutive makes them softer and more polite.

skeleton.note: indeclinable neuter noun, the target word

keyPoint: Шоу is an indeclinable neuter noun.

grammarFocus.construction: смотрю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + accusative (шоу, an indeclinable neuter noun)
grammarFocus.note: шоу is borrowed from English 'show' and never declines. It is grammatically neuter, so adjectives take neuter forms: новое шоу.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is смотрим
adding the neuter adjective новое (шоу itself is unchanged)

options.note: with передача ('programme'), the native Russian word
with сериал ('series'), more specific

paraphrases.simplest: Я смотрю шоу. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: Indeclinable neuter nouns (шоу, кино, метро, радио)
takeaway.note: They never change, so case comes from word order and modifiers. Most recent loanwords join this group.

keyPoint: Дедушка is grammatically masculine but declines like a feminine-type noun.

replies.gloss: Say hi to him for me.

grammarFocus.construction: the possessive мой (masculine) + дедушка (a masculine noun in -а) + the adverb дома, with zero copula
grammarFocus.note: Despite the -а ending, дедушка is masculine, so modifiers take masculine forms like мой. Its declension, however, follows the feminine pattern (дедушке, дедушку).

variations.note: with a grandmother, the possessive goes feminine: моя
with a plural subject (мои)

options.note: dropping the possessive and adding сейчас
stating it negatively: 'he hasn't gone anywhere'

paraphrases.simplest: Дедушка дома. — dropping the possessive is shortest and clear from context.

takeaway.pattern: Masculine nouns in -а / -я (дедушка, папа, дядя, мужчина)
takeaway.note: They decline like feminines but take masculine agreement: Мой дедушка пришёл. That mismatch is the point.

keyPoint: Мило is the adverbial form of the adjective милый.

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb мило (from милый via -о) + улыбается (reflexive imperfective present, 3rd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: The adjective милый ('sweet, kind') gives the adverb мило with -о. улыбаться always carries -ся.

variations.note: with a masculine subject (the verb form is unchanged)
the perfective past gives a single smile

options.note: using the noun улыбка with у + genitive
with приветливо ('warmly')

paraphrases.simplest: Она мило улыбается. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: улыбаться мне — the person smiled at goes in the dative. Keep улыбаться ('to smile') distinct from смеяться ('to laugh').

keyPoint: Какой-нибудь expresses an indefinite "any kind of."

grammarFocus.construction: the perfective imperative купи + the indefinite determiner какой-нибудь + accusative (хлеб — masculine inanimate, accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: какой-нибудь means 'any kind at all' and agrees with its noun in gender, number and case (какую-нибудь книгу).

variations.note: with a feminine noun: какую-нибудь книгу
formal or plural request uses купите

options.note: putting любой ('any') after the noun, more colloquial
что-нибудь + infinitive: 'something to eat'

paraphrases.simplest: Купи хлеб. — context already conveys 'any kind will do.'

takeaway.pattern: какой-нибудь (any kind) / какой-то (some particular but unidentified)
takeaway.note: Requests take какой-нибудь; 'for some reason' takes какой-то. The -нибудь / -то contrast runs through all these pronouns.

keyPoint: Арестовать is a biaspectual verb meaning "to arrest."

grammarFocus.construction: the short-form adjective должен + accusative (тебя, before the verb) + the infinitive of a biaspectual verb (арестовать)
grammarFocus.note: арестовать is biaspectual: one form covers both aspects, and only context tells you whether it's 'to arrest' as a single act or as a process.

variations.note: a female speaker uses должна
plural or formal

options.note: the short passive participle арестованы — the standard formula for making an arrest
using задержать ('to detain') with придётся

paraphrases.simplest: Вы арестованы. — the formula actually used when making an arrest.

takeaway.note: One form serves both aspects; context and time adverbs disambiguate.

skeleton.note: indeclinable feminine noun, the target word

keyPoint: Леди is an indeclinable feminine noun borrowed from English.

replies.gloss: Have you known each other long?

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the adjective добрая + the indeclinable feminine noun леди as nominative predicate
grammarFocus.note: леди is borrowed from English 'lady' and never declines, but it is grammatically feminine, so the adjective takes the feminine добрая.

variations.note: with человек (masculine) the adjective goes masculine: добрый
in the plural the adjective is добрые (леди stays unchanged)

options.note: with женщина, the native Russian word
dropping the noun and leaving just the adjective as predicate

paraphrases.simplest: Она очень добрая. — dropping the noun is the most natural and compact.

takeaway.pattern: The gender of an indeclinable noun shows in its modifier (добрая леди / новое шоу)
takeaway.note: леди is feminine, шоу and такси neuter. Since the noun never changes, the adjective carries gender and case.

keyPoint: Слушайте is formally an imperative but is used as an attention-getting interjection.

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + the imperfective imperative Слушайте, functioning as an attention-getter
grammarFocus.note: Literally 'listen,' but in conversation it works as an interjection — 'look, listen here' — opening a remark.

variations.note: the familiar singular слушай
the perfective послушайте stresses a single 'just listen a moment'

options.note: using the noun внимание ('attention'), formal
using привлечь внимание ('to attract attention') to report it

paraphrases.simplest: Слушай! — the natural way to get a friend's attention.

takeaway.note: Слушай, а ты не знаешь…? ('hey, do you happen to know…?') is an extremely common way to start a question.

skeleton.note: future 1st person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Позаботиться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "taking care of."

replies.gloss: I'll take care of you too.

grammarFocus.construction: позабочусь (reflexive perfective future, 1st person singular) + о + prepositional (тебе)
grammarFocus.note: заботиться / позаботиться mark whom you look after with о + prepositional. The perfective future makes it a promise.

variations.note: the prepositional вас for formal or plural address
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is позаботимся

options.ru: Я о тебе позабочусь, не волнуйся.
options.note: reordered and softened with не волнуйся
the negated оставить ('I won't abandon you'), more emotive

paraphrases.simplest: Я позабочусь о тебе. — the natural way to make this promise.

takeaway.pattern: заботиться о + prepositional ('to look after, to care about')
takeaway.note: заботиться о детях ('to look after children'), заботиться о здоровье ('to look after your health'). о + prepositional is obligatory.

keyPoint: Детка is an intimate term of endearment.

grammarFocus.construction: the casual greeting Привет + an affectionate address (детка, nominative)
grammarFocus.note: детка derives from ребёнок as a pet name and is reserved for partners or very close company. Forms of address take the nominative.

variations.note: with дорогая ('darling,' to a woman), gentler
with милый ('darling,' to a man)

options.note: using солнце ('sunshine') — a very Russian endearment
dropping the address, safe in any situation

paraphrases.simplest: Привет! — unless you're very close, the single word is safest.

takeaway.note: All of these belong to partners and family. Never use them at work or with someone you've just met.

keyPoint: Сойти is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "getting off."

grammarFocus.construction: dative (мне) + нужно + perfective infinitive (сойти) + the adverb здесь
grammarFocus.note: сойти means getting off a vehicle, with с + genitive for what you get off (сойти с автобуса). Dative + нужно + infinitive is the basic necessity frame.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural (dative нам)
adding на следующей ('at the next stop')

options.note: using выходить in the present — what people actually say on a bus or train
using the imperative of остановить to ask the driver

paraphrases.simplest: Я выхожу. — on public transport those two words are enough.

takeaway.pattern: сойти / выйти с + genitive (to get off a vehicle)
takeaway.note: Вы выходите? ('are you getting off?') is essential for working your way to the door on a crowded bus.

keyPoint: "Добро пожаловать" is a fixed greeting meaning "welcome."

grammarFocus.construction: the set greeting Добро пожаловать (the adverb добро plus an archaic infinitive пожаловать)
grammarFocus.note: Literally 'you have kindly come.' In modern Russian it's treated as a single unanalysed greeting; the destination is added with в + accusative.

variations.note: adding в + accusative for the place
with домой ('home')

options.note: using рады (short-form plural) + infinitive: 'glad to see you'
using the imperative of проходить to usher someone in

paraphrases.simplest: Добро пожаловать! — the set phrase, and the shortest.

takeaway.note: Everywhere on signs and in announcements; the destination takes в + accusative (в Россию, в наш дом).

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Клясться is imperfective, meaning "to swear/vow."

replies.gloss: You don't need to swear it.

grammarFocus.construction: клянусь (imperfective present, 1st person singular of клясться) + dative (тебе)
grammarFocus.note: клясться is reflexive and takes the person sworn to in the dative. It conjugates клянусь, клянёшься, with н appearing in the stem.

variations.note: the dative вам for formal or plural address
adding a что clause for what you swear to

options.note: a set phrase, 'honestly' — far the most common in speech
using обещать ('I promise'), milder

paraphrases.simplest: Честное слово! — the natural everyday way to insist you mean it.

takeaway.pattern: клясться + dative ('to swear to someone') / Честное слово ('honestly')
takeaway.note: клянусь is a heavy oath; for everyday 'honestly, it's true,' Честное слово fits better.

keyPoint: Мэм is an indeclinable honorific borrowed from English "ma'am."

replies.gloss: Who did she say that to?

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + the affirmative Да + the indeclinable borrowed address мэм
grammarFocus.note: мэм comes from English ma'am and never declines. It's virtually unused in Russian conversation, appearing mainly in translations and foreign settings.

variations.note: with the male form сэр
with конечно ('of course') instead — a genuinely Russian reply

options.note: with Хорошо ('all right'), the natural acknowledgement
using согласиться to report it indirectly

paraphrases.simplest: Она сказала: «Хорошо». — the natural version in a Russian setting.

takeaway.pattern: мэм and сэр belong to translated contexts only
takeaway.note: Real Russian address uses Девушка!, Молодой человек!, or first name plus patronymic (Иван Петрович).

keyPoint: Переводчик is an agent noun derived from перевести.

grammarFocus.construction: dative (мне) + нужен (short-form adjective, masculine singular) + nominative (переводчик, with the agent suffix -чик)
grammarFocus.note: In the нужен frame, what is needed stands in the nominative and нужен agrees with it. переводчик is перевести ('to translate') plus -чик — 'one who translates.'

variations.note: for a female interpreter: нужна переводчица
in the plural: нужны переводчики

options.note: explaining the situation so the need is obvious
using мочь + найти to make it a request

paraphrases.simplest: Мне нужен переводчик. — the most direct and effective line at any counter.

takeaway.note: They build person-nouns from verbs: переводить → переводчик, учить → учитель. A key to expanding vocabulary.

keyPoint: Эм is a colloquial filler word used while thinking.

grammarFocus.construction: the filler Эм (set off by a comma) + a negated imperfective present
grammarFocus.note: Эм is a colloquial filler buying time to think (English 'um'). It belongs only to speech and is set off by a comma.

variations.note: with Ну ('well'), the most common Russian filler
with a different continuation: 'I'll think about it'

options.note: даже softens it to 'I really don't know'
a set phrase, 'hard to say,' holding off an answer

paraphrases.simplest: Даже не знаю. — the natural way to express hesitation.

takeaway.pattern: Fillers (Ну / Эм / Как бы / Это самое)
takeaway.note: Ну is the most frequent. Overused they sound clumsy — set phrases like Даже не знаю or Трудно сказать fill the gap more gracefully.

keyPoint: Б is the colloquial shortened form of бы.

grammarFocus.construction: the conditional particle б (a colloquial clipping of бы) + the past form хотел — the Russian conditional
grammarFocus.note: The Russian conditional is formed with a past-tense verb plus бы. б is the spoken short form. Я бы хотел means 'I'd like,' a polite wish.

variations.note: a female speaker uses the past хотела
with a plural subject, хотели

options.note: the direct form without the conditional (a little blunt)
adding an accusative object to make it an order

paraphrases.simplest: Я бы хотел… — adding бы alone makes any request a notch more polite.

takeaway.pattern: past tense + бы (the conditional — polite wishes and unreal conditions)
takeaway.note: Я бы хотел ('I'd like'), Если бы я знал ('if I had known'). бы moves freely in the sentence, and б is its colloquial clipping.

keyPoint: Мадам is an indeclinable honorific borrowed from French madame.

grammarFocus.construction: прошу (1st person singular, subject dropped) + the indeclinable address мадам
grammarFocus.note: Прошу on its own is a courteous 'please, go ahead.' мадам is borrowed from French madame and never declines.

variations.note: adding проходите ('do come through') to spell it out
with the accusative вас and no form of address

options.note: пожалуйста plus an imperative — the standard way to usher someone in
with the imperative of входить ('to come in')

paraphrases.simplest: Пожалуйста. — one word is enough to usher someone through.

takeaway.pattern: Прошу ('please, go ahead' — a courteous invitation)
takeaway.note: Прошу covers both 'please' and 'after you.' мадам is rare in Russian; Девушка! is what people actually say.

skeleton.note: future 3rd person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Сработать is perfective, meaning a plan "works out" as a single outcome.

grammarFocus.construction: надеется (reflexive imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + a что clause + perfective future (сработает)
grammarFocus.note: надеяться is reflexive and takes what you hope for in a что clause. A perfective future in the clause makes it a hope for one definite outcome.

variations.note: with a 1st-person singular subject (надеюсь)
with a plural subject in the clause (сработают)

options.note: using верить в + accusative ('to believe in')
with получиться ('to work out'), more colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Надеюсь, получится. — the short version people actually use.

takeaway.pattern: надеяться, что + perfective future ('to hope that…')
takeaway.note: надеяться на + accusative ('to count on') is also frequent, and Надеюсь alone works as a parenthetical 'I hope.'

keyPoint: Смешно is the adverbial form of the adjective смешной.

replies.gloss: She has a good sense of humor.

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb смешно (from смешной via -о) + шутит (imperfective present, 3rd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: смешно means 'amusingly.' With a dative it also forms an impersonal predicate — Мне смешно ('I find it funny') — so the form does double duty.

variations.note: with a masculine subject
the dative + impersonal predicate use

options.note: using the noun phrase чувство юмора ('sense of humour')
using весело with с + instrumental ('she's always fun')

paraphrases.simplest: Она смешно шутит. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: смешно as adverb / Мне смешно as dative + impersonal predicate
takeaway.note: The same -о form serves both roles — compare Мне холодно and Мне интересно.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Таблетка is a feminine noun for "pill, tablet."

replies.gloss: Okay, I'll wash it down with water.

grammarFocus.construction: выпей (perfective imperative of выпить) + accusative (таблетку, a feminine noun in -у)
grammarFocus.note: выпить is вы- plus пить, 'to drink up.' For medicine, выпить таблетку and принять таблетку are the set phrases.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses выпейте
the feminine две governs the genitive singular таблетки

options.note: using принять ('to take'), the medical phrasing
dative + надо + infinitive, framed as a necessity

paraphrases.simplest: Выпей таблетку. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: выпить таблетку / принять лекарство ('to take medicine')
takeaway.note: выпить is colloquial, принять is what the leaflet says; пить лекарство is also everyday usage.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Завтрак is a masculine noun meaning "breakfast."

grammarFocus.construction: готовит (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + accusative (завтрак — masculine inanimate, accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: The imperfective present means it's underway. завтрак, обед and ужин are all masculine inanimate nouns.

variations.note: with a different meal (обед — lunch)
the perfective past gives the result: breakfast is made

options.note: using делать, more colloquial
the reflexive готовится ('is being made'), a passive framing

paraphrases.simplest: Она готовит завтрак. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: завтрак / обед / ужин with готовить (to make a meal)
takeaway.note: Learn the eating verbs alongside: завтракать, обедать, ужинать (Я завтракаю в семь).

skeleton.note: grammatically masculine but gender-neutral in use, the target word

keyPoint: Молодец is a term of praise used regardless of the addressee's gender.

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the noun predicate молодец, a compliment used regardless of gender
grammarFocus.note: молодец is grammatically masculine, but Ты молодец! is said to women too — an exception that doesn't change form for gender.

variations.note: with the formal вы, молодец still stays as is
for several people, the plural молодцы

options.note: using получиться to praise the result
using справиться ('to manage') for more specific praise

paraphrases.simplest: Молодец! — one word says it all.

takeaway.note: Singular молодец, plural молодцы. Women get the masculine form unchanged.

keyPoint: Отвезти is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "driving someone" somewhere.

grammarFocus.construction: можешь (2nd person singular of мочь) + perfective infinitive (отвезти) + accusative (меня) + the directional adverb домой
grammarFocus.note: отвезти is to take someone by vehicle. домой means 'homeward' and takes no preposition — note the contrast with дома ('at home').

variations.note: formal or plural address uses можете
в + accusative for a specific destination

options.note: using подвезти ('to give a lift') — the most natural, colloquial request

options.ru: Не мог бы ты отвезти меня домой?
options.note: the conditional не мог бы makes it markedly more polite

paraphrases.simplest: Подвезёшь меня? — with a friend, this one verb is the natural choice.

takeaway.note: отвезти домой vs быть дома — both adverbs, both without a preposition.

skeleton.note: neuter noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Расследование is a neuter noun meaning "investigation."

replies.gloss: Who turned out to be guilty?

grammarFocus.construction: смотрите (imperfective present, 2nd person plural) + accusative (сериал) + про + accusative (расследование)
grammarFocus.note: про is the colloquial 'about' and takes the accusative; it's preferred in speech over the written о + prepositional.

variations.note: with someone close it becomes ты смотришь
with о + prepositional, more written in register

options.note: using the noun детектив ('crime drama'), much shorter
keeping про + accusative but changing the subject matter

paraphrases.simplest: Вы смотрите детектив? — one genre word covers it, so this is shortest.

takeaway.note: книга про войну vs книга о войне — same meaning, different case.

keyPoint: Окей is a colloquial agreement particle borrowed from English "OK."

grammarFocus.construction: the agreement particle Окей (set off by a comma) + perfective past (понял)
grammarFocus.note: Окей is borrowed from English OK and is colloquial only. Я понял is perfective past: 'I've got it, just now.'

variations.note: a female speaker uses поняла
with Ладно, the native Russian particle

options.note: using понятно ('understood'), the standard reply
one word for 'got it' — very common

paraphrases.simplest: Ясно. — one word is a complete acknowledgement.

takeaway.note: Я понял is perfective — understood just now. Понятно and Ясно are impersonal and the easiest replies.

keyPoint: То is the neuter form of тот, meaning "that."

grammarFocus.construction: дай (perfective imperative of дать) + dative (мне) + accusative (то письмо, the neuter of тот)
grammarFocus.note: тот means 'that one over there' and pairs with этот ('this one'). Its neuter is то, its feminine та.

variations.note: with a feminine noun the accusative is ту книгу
switching to этот gives 'this letter'

options.note: using передать ('to pass') if it's out of reach
можно + accusative with no verb — a softer request

paraphrases.simplest: Дай мне то письмо. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: тот marks distance or something already mentioned: в тот день ('that day'), тот самый ('that very one').

skeleton.note: future 1st person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Сделать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "doing."

grammarFocus.construction: сделаю (perfective future, 1st person singular) + accusative (это) + the time adverb завтра
grammarFocus.note: A perfective conjugated in the present has future meaning (сделаю = 'I'll do it'). The imperfective future is the compound буду делать.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is сделаем
the imperfective future: 'I'll be working on it tomorrow'

options.note: using заняться + instrumental ('I'll get to it')
using оставить на + accusative ('I'll leave it for tomorrow')

paraphrases.simplest: Сделаю завтра. — dropping subject and object is what people say.

takeaway.pattern: Perfective present forms = future (сделаю) / imperfective future = буду + infinitive
takeaway.note: Russian has two futures: сделаю (will get it done) vs буду делать (will be doing it).

keyPoint: Спасибо originally meant "God save (you)" and functions as an interjection of thanks.

replies.gloss: What was she thanking you for?

grammarFocus.construction: сказала (perfective past, feminine singular) + dative (мне) + the interjection спасибо as object
grammarFocus.note: спасибо is an interjection, but in сказать спасибо it behaves like the verb's object. It contracts from «спаси Бог» ('God save you').

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is сказал
adding большое to strengthen the thanks

options.note: using поблагодарить + accusative, more formal
using the short-form adjective благодарна with a dative

paraphrases.simplest: Она поблагодарила меня. — one verb covers it, so this is tidier.

takeaway.note: спасибо puts the person in the dative (сказать спасибо маме), благодарить in the accusative (благодарить маму). The cases swap.

keyPoint: Ладно is a colloquial particle of agreement meaning "okay, fine."

grammarFocus.construction: the particle Ладно (set off by a comma) + perfective future (приду) + the time adverb завтра
grammarFocus.note: Ладно is a colloquial particle of grudging agreement — 'all right then.' приду is the irregular perfective future of прийти (приду, придёшь).

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is придём
with Хорошо, more neutral agreement

options.note: using Договорились ('agreed, then')
closing with до завтра ('see you tomorrow')

paraphrases.simplest: Ладно, приду. — dropping subject and time is what people say.

takeaway.note: Ладно concedes, Хорошо is neutral, Договорились confirms a deal. Pick by situation.

keyPoint: Чем is the conjunction meaning "than" in comparative constructions.

grammarFocus.construction: the comparative выше + the conjunction чем + nominative (я) — the comparative construction
grammarFocus.note: Russian has two comparatives: чем + nominative (Ты выше, чем я) and a bare genitive (Ты выше меня). With чем you need a comma.

variations.note: the genitive version — no чем, no comma
with both terms changed

options.note: adding на + accusative for the size of the difference
using the opposite comparative ниже and flipping the viewpoint

paraphrases.simplest: Ты выше меня. — the genitive version is shortest and most natural.

takeaway.note: Он старше, чем я = Он старше меня. The genitive version is shorter and more colloquial; чем requires a comma.

keyPoint: Со is a euphonic variant of с ("with") used before certain consonant clusters.

grammarFocus.construction: пойдём (perfective future, 1st person plural — a hortative) + со + instrumental (мной) + the adverb сейчас
grammarFocus.note: The perfective 1st plural works as 'let's.' The preposition с becomes со before мной for pronunciation (со мной, со всеми, со стола).

variations.note: the polite plural invitation пойдёмте
with a different instrumental (с нами keeps plain с)

options.note: the imperfective идём, more immediate
давай + perfective 1st plural softens it into a suggestion

paraphrases.simplest: Пойдём со мной. — already the simplest invitation.

takeaway.pattern: со мной / со всеми (a phonetic variant)
takeaway.note: с becomes со before awkward clusters like мной, всеми, стола; с тобой and с ним stay as they are.

keyPoint: Давай is a suggestion particle meaning "let's."

grammarFocus.construction: the hortative particle давай + perfective future 1st plural (выпьем) + accusative (кофе) + the adverb вместе
grammarFocus.note: давай plus a perfective 1st plural is the most natural 'let's.' давай is historically the imperative of давать but functions here as an invariable particle.

variations.note: the polite plural давайте
an imperfective infinitive shifts it to 'let's make a habit of it'

options.note: prefacing it with пойдём ('let's go'), more action-oriented
a negative question makes the offer more tentative

paraphrases.simplest: Давай выпьем кофе. — dropping вместе is shortest.

takeaway.note: Давай пойдём, Давайте начнём. давай never declines; only the polite давайте differs.

keyPoint: Привет is a casual greeting used among close acquaintances.

grammarFocus.construction: the greeting Привет + the interrogative adverb как + zero copula (как ты сегодня?)
grammarFocus.note: Как ты? ('how are you?') has no verb at all. Adding сегодня narrows it to today.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses вы
with Как дела?, the standard formula

options.note: the most common greeting pair
using настроение ('mood'), a touch more intimate

paraphrases.simplest: Привет! Как дела? — the natural greeting combination.

takeaway.pattern: Как дела? / Как ты? / Как вы? ('how are you?')
takeaway.note: All verbless zero-copula questions. Standard replies: Нормально, Хорошо, Так себе.

keyPoint: Об is the euphonic variant of о ("about") used before vowels.

grammarFocus.construction: думаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + об + prepositional (этом) + the frequency adverb часто
grammarFocus.note: The preposition о becomes об before a vowel (об этом, об отце). думать marks what you think about with о/об + prepositional.

variations.note: before a consonant it stays о (о тебе)
with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is думаем

options.ru: Это не выходит у меня из головы.
options.note: an idiom: 'it won't leave my head'
with вспоминать ('to recall')

paraphrases.simplest: Я часто об этом думаю. — just a reordering, and the most natural version.

takeaway.pattern: о before consonants / об before vowels (об этом, об отце, об одном)
takeaway.note: A purely phonetic variant. Learn обо мне as the third form (before мне).

skeleton.note: future 1st person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Смочь is the perfective partner of мочь, denoting a single instance of "being able to."

grammarFocus.construction: смогу (perfective future, 1st person singular of смочь) + perfective infinitive (прийти) with не
grammarFocus.note: смочь is the perfective of мочь — 'to manage to.' For future impossibility you need не смогу; не могу refers to the present.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject, не сможем
the imperfective не могу means 'I can't come right now'

options.note: using получиться ('it won't work out'), a softer refusal
к сожалению + не будет — a polite decline

paraphrases.simplest: Я не смогу прийти. — the clearest and most courteous way to decline.

takeaway.pattern: не могу (can't now) / не смогу (won't be able to)
takeaway.note: мочь is present ability, смочь a single future achievement. The standard decline is Я не смогу прийти.

keyPoint: Ни is a reinforcing negative particle used with the construction ни + genitive.

grammarFocus.construction: не + знать + the emphatic particle ни + genitive (слова) — total negation
grammarFocus.note: ни + genitive builds total negation ('not a single one'). It always accompanies the verbal не, and the object goes genitive: ни слова, ни разу.

variations.ru: Я не знаю ни одного слова.
variations.note: adding ни одного for even stronger emphasis
with a different verb: 'he didn't say a word'

options.note: using совсем не ('not at all') with a genitive
using the negative pronoun ничего

paraphrases.simplest: Я ничего не знаю. — the most common and compact total negation.

takeaway.pattern: не + verb + ни + genitive ('not a single…')
takeaway.note: ни слова ('not a word'), ни разу ('not once'), ни копейки ('not a kopeck'). The double negation with не is obligatory.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Иметь is an imperfective stative verb with no corresponding perfective partner.

grammarFocus.construction: имеешь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular of иметь) + accusative (право) + infinitive (знать)
grammarFocus.note: иметь means 'to have,' but everyday possession is normally у + genitive. иметь survives mainly in set phrases like иметь право.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses имеете
with a different infinitive: the right to remain silent

options.note: recast with у + genitive + есть, more colloquial
using вправе ('entitled'), compact and bookish

paraphrases.simplest: Ты имеешь право знать. — the natural formula for stating a right.

takeaway.pattern: иметь право + infinitive ('to have the right to…')
takeaway.note: иметь lives in set phrases: иметь право, иметь значение, иметь в виду. Everyday possession is У меня есть.

keyPoint: Пожалуйста grew out of the imperative of пожаловать and became fixed as the word for "please."

replies.gloss: Of course, what do you need?

grammarFocus.construction: помоги (perfective imperative of помочь) + dative (мне) + the particle пожалуйста
grammarFocus.note: помочь takes the person helped in the dative. пожалуйста is an invariable particle meaning both 'please' and 'you're welcome,' set off by a comma.

variations.note: formal or plural request uses помогите
with a different dative: 'help him'

options.ru: Не могли бы вы мне помочь?
options.note: the conditional не могли бы — the most polite request
using the noun помощь with dative + нужна

paraphrases.simplest: Помогите, пожалуйста! — in an emergency, these two words do the most.

takeaway.pattern: помочь + dative ('to help someone') / пожалуйста ('please, you're welcome')
takeaway.note: помочь takes the dative, not the accusative. пожалуйста works both for requests and as a reply to thanks.

keyPoint: Сюда is an adverb of direction meaning "to here."

grammarFocus.construction: the imperfective imperative иди + the directional adverb сюда + the emphatic прямо сейчас
grammarFocus.note: сюда means 'to here' (direction) while здесь means 'here' (location). прямо сейчас is a forceful 'right now.'

variations.note: formal or plural address uses идите
with a different direction (туда — over there)

options.note: подойти plus немедленно ('immediately') — a harder command
adding быстро, more colloquially urgent

paraphrases.simplest: Иди сюда! — strong enough even without прямо сейчас.

takeaway.note: Иди сюда ('come here') vs Я здесь ('I'm here'). Russian uses different adverbs for motion and position.

skeleton.note: interrogative pronoun, colloquial genitive, the target word

keyPoint: Чего is the genitive form of что, used colloquially to mean "what."

grammarFocus.construction: the interrogative чего (genitive of что) + хочешь (2nd person singular) + the adverb сейчас
grammarFocus.note: хотеть can take either the genitive or the accusative. Чего хочешь? is very common in speech, and Что хочешь? means the same.

variations.note: with the accusative что (virtually the same meaning)
formal or plural address uses хотите

options.note: dative + нужно — a more practical way to ask
the conditional хотелось бы + dative — the gentlest, most polite version

paraphrases.simplest: Что ты хочешь? — the clearest standard form.

takeaway.note: Чего ты хочешь? sounds colloquial and more charged; Что ты хочешь? is neutral. In negatives the genitive rules: Я не хочу ничего.

keyPoint: Значит is a parenthetical adverb meaning "so, that means."

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical conclusion-marker Значит (set off by a comma) + a negated perfective future (не придёшь) with question intonation
grammarFocus.note: Значит draws a conclusion from what was said — 'so, then.' It opens the sentence, followed by a comma.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses не придёте
with a different predicate: 'so you agree?'

options.note: with то есть ('that is'), more neutral
with выходит ('so it turns out'), more colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Значит, не придёшь? — dropping the subject is what people say.

takeaway.pattern: Значит / То есть / Выходит ('so, then' — confirming an inference)
takeaway.note: All three take up what the other person said to confirm a conclusion, and all sit at the front behind a comma.

keyPoint: Here всего means "only, just" — a restrictive adverb.

grammarFocus.construction: заплатила (perfective past, feminine singular) + the limiting particle всего + сто + genitive plural (рублей)
grammarFocus.note: всего means 'only, no more than.' Numerals like сто govern the genitive plural: сто рублей.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is заплатил
with a different numeral (двадцать also takes the genitive plural)

options.note: with только ('only'), more neutral

options.ru: Ей это обошлось в сто рублей.
options.note: using обойтись в + accusative ('it cost her')

paraphrases.simplest: Она заплатила сто рублей. — dropping всего is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: Numeral government: 2-4 + genitive singular, 5 and up + genitive plural
takeaway.note: два рубля (genitive singular), пять рублей and сто рублей (genitive plural). всего and только add the 'only.'

keyPoint: Мистер is an indeclinable honorific borrowed from English "Mr."

grammarFocus.construction: the indeclinable address мистер + слышите (imperfective present, 2nd person plural) + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: слышать means 'to hear' and takes the accusative. мистер is borrowed from English and never declines.

variations.note: with the form of address kept (the standard version here)
with Простите instead — how a Russian would actually open

options.note: dropping the form of address — the most natural check
on a call, the impersonal слышно ('can you hear')

paraphrases.simplest: Вы меня слышите? — Russian naturally drops the title.

takeaway.pattern: слышать + accusative (to hear) / слушать + accusative (to listen)
takeaway.note: слышать is sound reaching you; слушать is listening on purpose. Я слышу музыку vs Я слушаю музыку.

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Собираться is imperfective, expressing intention to do something soon (pairs with собраться).

grammarFocus.construction: собираюсь (reflexive imperfective present, 1st person singular) + the directional adverb домой
grammarFocus.note: собираться means 'to be about to, to get ready to' and takes an infinitive or a directional adverb. домой ('homeward') needs no preposition.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is собираемся
with an infinitive: 'I'm about to leave'

options.note: using the perfective future пойду, more definite
using пора ('it's time') with a directional adverb — the most natural version

paraphrases.simplest: Мне пора домой. — the natural way to announce you're heading off.

takeaway.note: Я собираюсь поехать expresses intention; keep it apart from собираться meaning 'to gather, to get ready.'

keyPoint: Сэр is an indeclinable honorific borrowed from English "sir."

grammarFocus.construction: the affirmative Да + the indeclinable address сэр + perfective past (понял)
grammarFocus.note: сэр is borrowed from English sir and never declines. Я понял is perfective past — understood just now.

variations.note: a female speaker uses поняла
with конечно instead of the title — a Russian-sounding reply

options.note: with понятно ('understood'), the standard reply
the set 'yes, sir' of the military and police

paraphrases.simplest: Да, понятно. — the natural reply in a Russian workplace.

takeaway.note: Так точно belongs to uniformed services. сэр isn't used in Russian — people use first name plus patronymic.

keyPoint: Остаться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "staying" (pairs with оставаться).

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + perfective infinitive (остаться) + the locative adverb дома
grammarFocus.note: остаться is a reflexive perfective, 'to stay, to remain.' дома means 'at home' (location), paired with домой ('homeward').

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject the verb is хотим
with a different locative adverb

options.note: лучше ('I'd rather') with the perfective future — more natural
the negated хочется + dative: 'I don't feel like going anywhere'

paraphrases.simplest: Я останусь дома. — dropping хочу is shorter and clearer.

takeaway.note: остаться дома vs пойти домой — location and direction take different adverbs.

keyPoint: Немного is a quantity adverb meaning "a little," combined with the genitive case.

grammarFocus.construction: дай (perfective imperative) + dative (мне) + the quantity adverb немного + partitive genitive (воды)
grammarFocus.note: немного governs the genitive. Liquids and uncountables take the partitive genitive (воды, хлеба, денег) for 'some water.'

variations.note: formal or polite request uses дайте
the accusative points to that particular water

options.note: можно + partitive genitive with no verb — the lightest request
with налить ('to pour'), more specific

paraphrases.simplest: Можно воды? — the shortest, most natural way to ask for water.

takeaway.pattern: Partitive genitive (немного воды / чашка чая / много денег)
takeaway.note: Quantity words take the genitive. Compare Дай воду ('that water') with Дай воды ('some water').

keyPoint: Увидеть is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "seeing" (pairs with видеть).

replies.gloss: I want to see you too.

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + accusative (тебя, before the verb) + perfective infinitive (увидеть)
grammarFocus.note: увидеть is the perfective 'to catch sight of,' as against видеть ('to see,' a state). Pronoun objects naturally precede the verb.

variations.note: with the formal or plural accusative вас
the imperfective видеть makes it an ongoing wish to see you

options.note: using встретиться с + instrumental, implying an arrangement
давай with the reciprocal perfective turns it into an invitation

paraphrases.simplest: Давай увидимся. — the natural way to propose meeting up.

takeaway.pattern: видеть (to see, a state) / увидеть (to catch sight of, one moment)
takeaway.note: Я вижу ('I can see') vs Я увидел ('I spotted'). The same state/moment split as знать/узнать and помнить/вспомнить.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Заниматься is imperfective, meaning "to be occupied with" and taking the instrumental case (pairs with заняться).

grammarFocus.construction: the interrogative чем (instrumental of что) + занимаешься (reflexive imperfective present, 2nd person singular)
grammarFocus.note: заниматься means 'to be occupied with' and takes the instrumental. Чем ты занимаешься? asks both 'what are you doing?' and 'what do you do for a living?'

variations.note: formal or plural занимаетесь — the standard way to ask someone's occupation
answering with the instrumental: 'I'm studying Russian'

options.note: using делать + accusative to ask about the present activity
работать + instrumental for occupation (кем — 'as what')

paraphrases.simplest: Что ты делаешь? — simpler if you only mean the present moment.

takeaway.pattern: заниматься + instrumental / Чем вы занимаетесь? ('what do you do?')
takeaway.note: A key instrumental verb — and the natural way to ask about someone's work when you first meet.

keyPoint: Пора is an impersonal predicate meaning "it's time (to)."

grammarFocus.construction: the impersonal predicate пора + infinitive (идти) + the directional adverb домой
grammarFocus.note: пора means 'it's time to' and takes an infinitive. The person involved is added in the dative (Мне пора идти).

variations.note: adding the dative мне to name who it concerns
dropping the verb: dative + пора + directional adverb

options.note: using dative + нужно + infinitive
perfective future plus a reason — the natural way to take your leave

paraphrases.simplest: Мне пора. — two words for 'I have to go.'

takeaway.note: Мне пора is the standard way to wrap up a conversation, and it works with no verb at all.

keyPoint: Кажется is the 3rd person singular of казаться, used as a parenthetical meaning "it seems."

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical кажется (set off by a comma) + знаю (imperfective present, 1st person singular) + accusative (тебя)
grammarFocus.note: кажется means 'it seems' and opens the sentence behind a comma. Adding a dative gives Мне кажется.

variations.note: with the dative мне — the fuller version
with the short-form adjective знакомы ('we've met')

options.note: using встречаться ('we've met somewhere') — the most natural version
using видеть with где-то ('somewhere')

paraphrases.simplest: Мы где-то встречались? — the natural opener when you half-recognise someone.

takeaway.note: The key hedging phrase. казаться takes a dative, and its predicate goes instrumental (Он кажется умным).

keyPoint: Оставить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "leaving/letting be" (pairs with оставлять).

grammarFocus.construction: оставь (perfective imperative) + accusative (меня) + в + prepositional (покое) — a set phrase
grammarFocus.note: оставить в покое means 'to leave someone alone.' покой takes the prepositional покое.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses оставьте
with a different accusative: 'leave him alone'

options.note: the negated imperative of трогать ('don't touch, don't bother me')
дать + infinitive: 'let me have some time alone' — gentler

paraphrases.simplest: Оставь меня в покое. — the set phrase, and the most forceful.

takeaway.pattern: оставить в покое ('to leave alone' — a fixed phrase)
takeaway.note: Learn оставить + accusative + в покое as a unit; Дай мне побыть одному is the gentler alternative.

keyPoint: Извинить is perfective, meaning "to forgive" (pairs with извинять).

grammarFocus.construction: извини (perfective imperative) + accusative (меня) + за + accusative (это)
grammarFocus.note: извинить takes the person forgiven in the accusative and the reason in за + accusative — the same frame as простить.

variations.note: formal or plural apology uses извините
dropping меня and keeping just the reason — the most natural version

options.note: with простить, a weightier apology
dative + жаль to express regret

paraphrases.simplest: Извини за это. — dropping меня is the natural version.

takeaway.note: Извини за опоздание, за беспокойство, за задержку — за + accusative is the standard way to name the reason.

keyPoint: Подождать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "waiting a bit" (pairs with ждать).

grammarFocus.construction: подожди (perfective imperative) + accusative (меня) + accusative of duration (одну минуту)
grammarFocus.note: подождать can take its object in either the accusative or genitive. Duration goes in the accusative with no preposition (одну минуту, два часа).

variations.note: formal or plural request uses подождите
with немного ('a bit'), leaving the time vague

options.note: dropping the verb — the most compact set phrase
'I'll be quick, hang on' — split into two clauses

paraphrases.simplest: Одну минуту! — enough on its own for 'just a moment.'

takeaway.pattern: Duration takes the bare accusative (одну минуту / два часа / всю неделю)
takeaway.note: Duration is accusative; clock time is в + accusative (в два часа). That split is the core of time expressions.

keyPoint: Подумать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "thinking it over a bit" (pairs with думать).

grammarFocus.construction: дай (perfective imperative) + dative (мне) + perfective infinitive (подумать) + the adverb немного
grammarFocus.note: дать + dative + infinitive means 'let someone do something.' подумать, with по-, means thinking for a little while.

variations.note: formal or polite request uses дайте
inserting the accusative время for a fuller phrasing

options.note: using dative + нужно + infinitive
perfective future: 'I'll think and let you know'

paraphrases.simplest: Дай подумать. — dropping мне still works.

takeaway.pattern: дать + dative + infinitive ('let someone do something')
takeaway.note: Дай мне сказать ('let me speak'), Дайте пройти ('let me through'). A core way to ask permission.

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Чувствовать is imperfective, meaning "to feel" (pairs with почувствовать).

grammarFocus.construction: чувствовать себя (a fixed phrase with the reflexive себя) + the adverb плохо
grammarFocus.note: To describe how you feel, use чувствовать себя plus an adverb — плохо, хорошо, нормально — never an adjective.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person singular subject (себя is invariable)
with the comparative лучше ('better')

options.note: dative + the impersonal плохо — the shortest version
using the perfective past of заболеть ('I've fallen ill')

paraphrases.simplest: Мне плохо. — the shortest way to say you feel unwell.

takeaway.pattern: чувствовать себя + adverb / Мне плохо (the dative construction)
takeaway.note: Как вы себя чувствуете? ('how are you feeling?') is essential at a doctor's. себя is always there.

keyPoint: Черта is a feminine noun meaning "trait, feature."

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (тебя) + nominative (интересная черта, feminine agreement)
grammarFocus.note: черта ('trait, line') is a hard-stem feminine noun. In this есть-less possessive the adjective интересная agrees as feminine singular nominative.

variations.note: in the plural both adjective and noun take nominative plural
with a 3rd-person masculine possessor

options.note: adding характера ('of character') to be specific
using по-своему ('in your own way') to appraise the whole person

paraphrases.simplest: У тебя интересная черта. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: черта means both 'trait' and 'line' — черты лица ('facial features') is another frequent use.

keyPoint: Дома is a location adverb meaning "at home," distinct from the directional домой ("homeward").

grammarFocus.construction: nominative (мама) + the time adverb сейчас + the locative adverb дома, with zero copula
grammarFocus.note: No verb for 'to be' in the present. The notable point is that дома means 'at home' and takes no preposition.

variations.note: in the past the copula была appears
another location takes на + prepositional (дома is the adverbial exception)

options.note: dropping сейчас — the shortest version
stating it negatively: 'she hasn't gone anywhere'

paraphrases.simplest: Мама дома. — shortest and most natural.

takeaway.pattern: дома is an adverb and takes no preposition
takeaway.note: Different from в доме ('inside the building'). Learn дома / домой / из дома as a set.

keyPoint: Три is a numeral; with the numbers 2-4 the noun takes the singular genitive form.

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (меня) + the numeral три + genitive singular (брата)
grammarFocus.note: два, три and четыре put the following noun in the genitive singular (три брата); five and up take the genitive plural (пять братьев).

variations.note: with five and up, the genitive plural братьев
feminine nouns follow the same rule: the genitive singular сестры

options.note: using the collective numeral четверо for family size
conveying it without a number

paraphrases.simplest: У меня три брата. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: 2-4 + genitive singular / 5 and up + genitive plural
takeaway.note: два брата vs пять братьев, две сестры vs пять сестёр — the single most important numeral rule in Russian.

keyPoint: Вещь is a feminine noun meaning "thing," with soft-stem declension endings.

grammarFocus.construction: купила (perfective past, feminine singular) + accusative (полезную вещь — a feminine noun in -ь, accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Feminine nouns in -ь like вещь don't change in the accusative; only the adjective ending полезную marks the case.

variations.note: in the plural: полезные вещи (inanimate, so accusative = nominative)
with a normally declining feminine noun, the noun changes too

options.note: что-то with a neuter adjective, vaguer
using the noun покупка ('purchase') to appraise it

paraphrases.simplest: Она купила полезную вещь. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: Feminine nouns in -ь (вещь, речь, мысль) have accusative = nominative
takeaway.note: Only the adjective's -ую reveals the accusative — a decisive clue when reading.

keyPoint: Отлично is the adverbial form of the adjective отличный, meaning "excellently."

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb отлично (from отличный via -о) + готовит (imperfective present, 3rd person singular) + accusative (кофе, indeclinable)
grammarFocus.note: отлично means 'excellently' and appraises skill. The imperfective present is what expresses 'is good at.'

variations.note: with a masculine subject
with хорошо ('well'), a more measured compliment

options.note: using у + genitive with an adjective
a dash construction with the superlative лучший

paraphrases.simplest: Она отлично готовит кофе. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: imperfective present + adverb ('to be good at')
takeaway.note: Она отлично готовит, Ты хорошо поёшь — ability always takes the imperfective present.

keyPoint: Похоже functions as a parenthetical meaning "apparently, it seems."

grammarFocus.construction: the parenthetical похоже (set off by commas) + perfective past (пришла) + the adverb уже
grammarFocus.note: похоже means 'it looks like' and is more evidence-based than кажется. It takes commas on both sides.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is пришёл
with the parenthetical at the front

options.note: with кажется, more subjective
with видимо ('apparently'), somewhat more formal

paraphrases.simplest: Похоже, она уже пришла. — the natural way to hedge this guess.

takeaway.note: похоже rests on evidence, кажется on impression, видимо leans to the written register.

skeleton.note: future 3rd person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Прийтись is a perfective impersonal verb meaning "to be forced to" (pairs with приходиться).

replies.gloss: Why does she have to leave?

grammarFocus.construction: знает + a colon introducing the content + dative (ей) + придётся (impersonal perfective future) + infinitive (уйти)
grammarFocus.note: придётся means 'will have to' and is impersonal: the person goes in the dative and there is no subject at all.

variations.note: with a 3rd-person masculine dative (ему)
the past пришлось: 'she had to leave'

options.ru: Она знает, что ей нужно уйти.
options.note: a что clause with нужно, more neutral

options.ru: У неё нет выбора — надо уходить.
options.note: spelling out the reason: 'she has no choice'

paraphrases.simplest: Ей придётся уйти. — dropping the main clause is shortest and clearest.

takeaway.note: Мне придётся работать. The past is пришлось; present necessity is нужно or надо.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Выглядеть is a stative verb of appearance with no perfective counterpart.

grammarFocus.construction: выглядишь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular) + the adverb хорошо + the time adverb сегодня
grammarFocus.note: выглядеть means 'to look' and takes an adverb (выглядеть хорошо) — in contrast to казаться, which takes the instrumental.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses выглядите
the exception: a state adjective takes the instrumental (уставшим)

options.note: with отлично, a stronger compliment
using идти + dative ('this look suits you')

paraphrases.simplest: Хорошо выглядишь! — dropping subject and time makes the best compliment.

takeaway.pattern: выглядеть + adverb ('to look') / казаться + instrumental ('to seem')
takeaway.note: выглядеть хорошо vs казаться умным — different case government, so learn them together.

keyPoint: Послушать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "listening a bit" (pairs with слушать).

grammarFocus.construction: послушай (perfective imperative) + accusative (эту песню, feminine -у)
grammarFocus.note: послушать, with по-, means giving something a listen. The feminine песня has the accusative песню.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses послушайте
the imperfective слушай makes it 'keep listening to it'

options.note: with включить ('put it on'), more concrete
услышать + надо: 'you have to hear this'

paraphrases.simplest: Послушай эту песню. — the natural way to recommend it.

takeaway.pattern: послушать (to give a listen) / слушать (to listen on)
takeaway.note: Послушай! ('listen a moment') also opens conversations. The prefix по- gives it that 'just once' sense.

keyPoint: Прямо is an adverb meaning "straight, directly."

replies.gloss: What do you want to say?

grammarFocus.construction: смотри (imperfective imperative) + the emphatic adverb прямо + на + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: смотреть marks what you look at with на + accusative. прямо ('straight') sharpens the direction.

variations.note: formal or plural address uses смотрите
with в + accusative: 'look straight in the eye'

options.note: the perfective посмотри: 'take a look at me'
the negated отводить глаза ('don't look away')

paraphrases.simplest: Смотри на меня. — dropping прямо is shortest.

takeaway.note: Note the two patterns: смотреть на картину ('look at a picture') but смотреть телевизор ('watch television,' direct accusative).

keyPoint: Давайте is the formal/plural form of давай, meaning "let's."

grammarFocus.construction: the hortative particle давайте + perfective future 1st plural (поговорим) + об + prepositional (этом)
grammarFocus.note: давайте plus a perfective 1st plural is the polite 'let's.' поговорить marks its topic with о/об + prepositional, and о becomes об before a vowel.

variations.note: with someone close, the singular давай
обсудить takes a direct accusative, so о disappears

options.note: using dative + надо + infinitive
можно + infinitive — a more tentative opener

paraphrases.simplest: Давайте поговорим. — dropping об этом is shortest.

takeaway.note: давай for friends, давайте for politeness or plural. Note too that поговорить takes о + prepositional while обсудить takes the accusative.

keyPoint: Несколько is a quantity determiner meaning "a few," combined with the genitive plural.

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (меня) + the quantifier несколько + genitive plural (вопросов)
grammarFocus.note: несколько ('several') governs the genitive plural, as do много, мало and сколько.

variations.note: with a different noun (genitive plural идей)
with много ('many'), likewise genitive plural

options.note: using пара ('a couple') + genitive to ask permission
the conditional with кое-что, more polite

paraphrases.simplest: У меня несколько вопросов. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: несколько / много / мало / сколько + genitive plural
takeaway.note: Quantifiers always take the genitive: несколько вопросов, много людей, сколько денег (genitive singular for uncountables).

keyPoint: Ага is a colloquial interjection of affirmation/agreement.

grammarFocus.construction: the affirmative interjection Ага (set off by a comma) + the time adverb теперь + perfective past (понял)
grammarFocus.note: Ага is a colloquial 'ah, I see.' теперь means 'now, at this point' and implies a change from before, unlike сейчас.

variations.note: a female speaker uses поняла
with А ('ah') + понятно, more neutral

options.note: dropping the interjection — the standard version
a set phrase: 'so that's it!'

paraphrases.simplest: Теперь понятно. — the natural way to signal you've got it.

takeaway.pattern: теперь ('now, as of now') / сейчас ('right now')
takeaway.note: теперь contrasts with before; сейчас is the point in time. Теперь я понял is the classic use.

keyPoint: Добрый is an adjective meaning "kind."

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the intensifier очень + adjective + noun predicate (добрый человек, nominative)
grammarFocus.note: A noun-phrase predicate stays in the nominative. добрый agrees with человек as masculine singular nominative.

variations.note: addressing a woman, both adjective and noun go feminine
for several people, the nominative plural добрые люди

options.note: dropping человек and leaving the adjective as predicate
using сердце ('heart') with у + genitive, more lyrical

paraphrases.simplest: Ты очень добрый. — dropping человек is the most natural.

takeaway.note: The standard way to appraise someone. In the past it shifts: Ты был добрым человеком (instrumental).

skeleton.note: 3rd person plural present, the target word

keyPoint: "Как тебя зовут" literally means "what do they call you," a fixed expression using звать to ask someone's name.

grammarFocus.construction: the interrogative как + accusative (тебя) + зовут (3rd person plural, used impersonally) — the formula for asking a name
grammarFocus.note: Literally 'how do they call you.' The subjectless 3rd plural зовут is the standard way to ask someone's name.

variations.note: the accusative вас for formal or plural address
asking about a third person

options.note: the imperative of представиться — formal
just the noun имя — short but blunt

paraphrases.simplest: Как тебя зовут? — the standard, natural way to ask.

takeaway.pattern: Как тебя / вас зовут? ('what's your name?') / Меня зовут… ('my name is…')
takeaway.note: The answer uses the same impersonal frame: Меня зовут Анна (accusative + зовут). Я Анна works too.

keyPoint: Должно is an impersonal predicate meaning "should" or "must be."

grammarFocus.construction: считает + a что clause + the impersonal predicate должно (neuter short form) + perfective infinitive (получиться)
grammarFocus.note: должно получиться means 'it should work out.' It is impersonal — no subject, and должно is fixed in the neuter.

variations.note: with a masculine subject
making всё the subject with a perfective future — more natural

options.note: using думать with выйти ('to work out')
using the short-form уверена with в + prepositional

paraphrases.simplest: Она думает, что получится. — what people actually say.

takeaway.pattern: должно получиться ('it should work out' — impersonal)
takeaway.note: должен/должна/должно/должны agree with a subject, but impersonally it's always neuter должно. Должно быть ('it must be') works the same way.

keyPoint: Уверен is the short form of уверенный, used in predicate position to mean "certain, sure."

grammarFocus.construction: the short-form adjective уверен (predicate) + в + prepositional (этом), with question intonation
grammarFocus.note: уверен is predicate-only and agrees in gender and number (уверен/уверена/уверены). What you're sure of takes в + prepositional.

variations.note: addressing a woman: уверена
formal or plural: уверены

options.note: using точно with знать, more colloquial
'is that definite?' — the shortest check

paraphrases.simplest: Ты уверен? — dropping в этом is shortest.

takeaway.note: Я уверен в себе ('I'm confident'), Я не уверен ('I'm not sure'). Don't forget the short-form agreement.

keyPoint: Ребята is a colloquial plural noun meaning "guys, folks."

grammarFocus.construction: позвала (perfective past, feminine singular) + accusative (ребят — animate plural, accusative = genitive) + на + accusative (ужин)
grammarFocus.note: ребята is a plural noun for 'the guys, everyone'; being animate, its accusative is ребят. What you invite someone to takes на + accusative.

variations.note: with a masculine subject the past is позвал
with a different animate plural (друзей)

options.note: using пригласить ('to invite'), more formal
using для + genitive ('for the guys')

paraphrases.simplest: Она позвала ребят на ужин. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: позвать / пригласить + accusative + на + accusative ('to invite to')
takeaway.note: позвать is colloquial, приглашать formal. And note the animate plural accusative = genitive (ребят, друзей).

keyPoint: Жаль is an impersonal predicate meaning "it's a pity, I'm sorry."

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + dative (мне) + the impersonal predicate жаль — 'I'm sorry'
grammarFocus.note: жаль takes no subject; the person feeling it goes in the dative. It shares a root with жалеть but exists only as a predicate.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural dative
adding очень — the most natural version

options.note: using извиниться to report it indirectly
with Простите, a more direct apology

paraphrases.simplest: Мне жаль. — two words for 'I'm sorry.'

takeaway.pattern: dative + жаль ('I'm sorry, it's a shame')
takeaway.note: Мне жаль ('I'm sorry'), Мне жаль его ('I feel sorry for him' — accusative). Also the phrase for condolences.

keyPoint: Туда is an adverb of direction meaning "to there."

grammarFocus.construction: хочу (1st person singular of хотеть) + the directional adverb туда + infinitive (идти) with не
grammarFocus.note: туда means 'to there' (direction), paired with там ('there,' location). The negated не хочу denies the intention.

variations.note: with a 1st-person plural subject, не хотим
with the locative там: 'I don't want to stay there'

options.note: хочется + dative — softer
offering an alternative with лучше

paraphrases.simplest: Я не хочу туда. — the infinitive can be dropped.

takeaway.note: идти туда vs быть там — direction and position take different adverbs.

keyPoint: Действительно is a confirming adverb meaning "really, actually."

grammarFocus.construction: the adverb действительно ('really') + the adverb так + думаешь (imperfective present, 2nd person singular), with question intonation
grammarFocus.note: действительно means 'really, in fact' and in a question it sharpens surprise. так means 'that way, so.'

variations.note: formal or plural address uses думаете
with правда ('really'), more colloquial

options.note: using серьёзно — the shortest expression of surprise
неужели ('surely not') conveys stronger disbelief

paraphrases.simplest: Ты серьёзно? — two words carry both surprise and the question.

takeaway.note: действительно is the most formal, правда colloquial, неужели the most incredulous.

skeleton.note: future 3rd person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Хватит is the future form of the perfective хватить, used as a fixed phrase meaning "enough, stop."

grammarFocus.construction: direct speech + the impersonal predicate Хватит + imperfective infinitive (спорить) — 'that's enough of…'
grammarFocus.note: Хватит is the 3rd singular of хватить used impersonally; it takes an infinitive to call a stop, and can also take a genitive (Хватит разговоров).

variations.note: with a different infinitive: 'stop shouting'
with the genitive plural споров: 'enough arguing'

options.note: using the imperative of перестать — more standard
Довольно ('enough') as a one-word set phrase

paraphrases.simplest: Хватит! — one word for 'that's enough.'

takeaway.pattern: Хватит + imperfective infinitive or genitive ('enough of…')
takeaway.note: Хватит болтать ('stop chattering'), Хватит с меня ('I've had enough'). Impersonal, so no subject.

keyPoint: Использовать is a biaspectual verb meaning "to use."

replies.gloss: What do you need it for?

grammarFocus.construction: можно (impersonal predicate) + the biaspectual infinitive использовать + accusative (твой телефон)
grammarFocus.note: использовать is biaspectual — one form for both aspects. It takes the accusative, in contrast to пользоваться, which takes the instrumental.

variations.note: adding the dative мне to name who's asking
воспользоваться takes the instrumental and sounds more polite

options.note: using с + genitive ('call from your phone'), more specific
дать + accusative — the most colloquial request

paraphrases.simplest: Можно твой телефон? — dropping the verb is shortest and natural.

takeaway.pattern: использовать + accusative vs пользоваться + instrumental (both 'to use')
takeaway.note: The key case contrast: использовать возможность vs пользоваться телефоном.

skeleton.note: future 1st person plural, the target word

keyPoint: Поехать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "setting off" by vehicle (pairs with ехать).

grammarFocus.construction: the hortative particle давай + perfective future 1st plural (поедем) + на + accusative (море)
grammarFocus.note: поехать is travelling by vehicle. 'To the sea' is на море (на + accusative) — never в море.

variations.note: the polite plural давайте
with a destination that takes в + accusative

options.note: the past поехали works colloquially as 'let's go!'
как насчёт + genitive ('how about…?') — a tentative suggestion

paraphrases.simplest: Поехали на море! — the most colloquial way to propose it.

takeaway.pattern: на море / на дачу (destinations taking на + accusative)
takeaway.note: на море and на работу take на; в Москву and в деревню take в. Each destination fixes its own preposition.

keyPoint: Больший is the comparative form of большой, meaning "greater."

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (меня) + the long-form comparative adjective больший + nominative (опыт)
grammarFocus.note: больший is the long-form comparative of большой and can modify a noun directly (больший опыт); as a predicate you use больше.

variations.note: the predicative comparative больше with the genitive опыта — the usual version
with a 3rd-person masculine possessor

options.note: the one-word comparative of опытный

options.ru: У меня больше опыта, чем у него.
