takeaway.pattern: terms of abuse are worth recognising, not using (ублюдок, негодяй, подонок)
takeaway.note: All of them insult someone severely and will damage the relationship. Quoting one to ask whether it was said stays neutral.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, prepositional, the target word

keyPoint: Колледж is a masculine noun meaning "college."

grammarFocus.construction: учиться (imperfective past plural учились) + в + prepositional (колледже)
grammarFocus.note: учиться means 'to study, be enrolled', with the institution in в + prepositional. колледж ends in -ж, giving the prepositional колледже.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты учился
A different prepositional: at university

options.ru: У вас есть колледж за плечами?
options.note: Using за плечами (have you got college behind you?), colloquial
Asking about образование (what's your education?), more general

paraphrases.simplest: Вы учились в колледже? — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: учиться в + prepositional (study at) / учить + accusative (teach or learn)
takeaway.note: Я учусь в школе (I'm at school), Я учу русский (I'm learning Russian), Он учит детей (he teaches children).

keyPoint: Коп is a colloquial masculine noun borrowed from English "cop."

grammarFocus.construction: знать (2pl знаете) + что clause + значить (3sg значит) + a quoted word («коп»)
grammarFocus.note: коп is slang for a police officer, borrowed from English 'cop'. что значит «...» is the set way to ask what a word means.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты знаешь

variations.ru: Вы знаете, что значит это слово?
variations.note: With это слово (this word)

options.note: Using что такое (what is a 'cop'?), the shortest question
Using переводиться (how does 'cop' translate?)

paraphrases.simplest: Что такое «коп»? — three words ask the same thing.

takeaway.pattern: что значит «...» (what does ... mean) / что такое ... (what is ...)
takeaway.note: что значит asks about a word's sense, что такое about the thing itself. коп is the slang counterpart of полицейский.

keyPoint: Опаздывать is imperfective, meaning "to be late" (pairs with опоздать).

replies.gloss: I try not to be late too.

grammarFocus.construction: negation не + любить (1sg люблю) + imperfective infinitive (опаздывать)
grammarFocus.note: любить plus an imperfective infinitive means 'to like doing'. Negated, it states a standing dislike. опаздывать means 'to be late'.

variations.note: A different infinitive: I don't like waiting
First person plural: не любим

options.note: Stated positively with вовремя (I'm always on time)
Making the noun опоздания the subject

paraphrases.simplest: Я не люблю опаздывать. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: It states a habit or disposition, so the imperfective is required: Я люблю гулять (I like walking). A perfective would make it a single act and sound wrong.

keyPoint: Здравствуй comes from the imperative of здравствовать ("to be healthy") and is a greeting for close acquaintances.

grammarFocus.construction: говорить (2pl говорите) + a quoted greeting («здравствуй»)
grammarFocus.note: здравствуй greets someone you address as ты; for вы and plural use здравствуйте. It began life as an imperative meaning 'be healthy'.

variations.note: With the polite form of the greeting
With привет (hi), informal

options.note: Using здороваться (how do you greet people?)
Asking на «ты» or на «вы» (do you use the familiar or polite form?)

paraphrases.simplest: Вы говорите «здравствуй»? — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: здравствуй (to ты) / здравствуйте (to вы and plural)
takeaway.note: привет (casual) < здравствуй (friendly but polite) < здравствуйте (most polite). Choose by your distance from the listener.

keyPoint: ФБР is an indeclinable acronym for Федеральное бюро расследований (Federal Bureau of Investigation).

replies.ru: Нет, но у меня друг там работает.
replies.gloss: No, but a friend of mine works there.

grammarFocus.construction: работать (imperfective present 2pl работаете) + в + prepositional (ФБР, an indeclinable acronym)
grammarFocus.note: Your place of work goes in в + prepositional. Acronyms like ФБР never change form (в ФБР, из ФБР).

variations.note: With an ordinary noun: do you work for the police?
To someone you address as ты: ты работаешь

options.note: Using из + genitive (are you from the FBI?) — the shortest check
Using агент with a genitive

paraphrases.simplest: Вы из ФБР? — three words ask the same thing.

takeaway.pattern: acronyms don't decline (в ФБР, в МГУ, по СМС)
takeaway.note: They take a gender but keep one form. работать в + prepositional is the basic frame for naming a workplace.

keyPoint: Сынок is an affectionate diminutive of сын (son).

grammarFocus.construction: the vocative noun Сынок (set off by a comma) + imperfective imperative (иди) + directional adverb сюда
grammarFocus.note: сынок is the diminutive of сын, used affectionately by an older person to a young man. A form of address stays in the nominative, marked off by a comma.

variations.note: To a girl: дочка
With подойти к + dative (come over to me)

options.note: The address placed last, which sounds gentler
Adding the particle -ка to soften the command

paraphrases.simplest: Иди сюда. — dropping the address is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: forms of address stay nominative and take commas (Сынок, иди сюда)
takeaway.note: Diminutives like сынок, дочка and мамочка convey warmth. сынок is used to young men generally, not only to one's own son.

keyPoint: Расслабиться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "relaxing" (pairs with расслабляться).

replies.gloss: What would you like to do?

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть (2pl хотите) + perfective infinitive (расслабиться)
grammarFocus.note: расслабиться is a reflexive perfective meaning 'to relax'; the transitive расслабить means 'to loosen'. The -ся decides which.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты хочешь
With dative + нужно (you need to relax)

options.note: Using отдохнуть (would you like to rest?), simpler
Using может with сделаем паузу (shall we take a break?)

paraphrases.simplest: Хотите отдохнуть? — two words carry the same intent.

takeaway.note: Расслабься! (relax!) is a conversational staple. расслабить мышцы (loosen the muscles) shows the transitive use.

keyPoint: Ошибаться is imperfective, meaning "to be wrong" (pairs with ошибиться).

grammarFocus.construction: мочь (2sg можешь) + imperfective infinitive (ошибаться)
grammarFocus.note: ошибаться is a reflexive imperfective meaning 'to be mistaken'. мочь plus an imperfective infinitive states a possibility.

variations.note: To a formal or plural addressee: можете
The perfective past gives 'you may have made a mistake'

options.note: Using не прав (you may be wrong)
Turned into a question with а если (and what if you're wrong?)

paraphrases.simplest: Ты можешь ошибаться. — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: Я ошибся (I was wrong), ошибаться номером (dial the wrong number). Being reflexive, it takes no object.

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Гордиться is a stative imperfective verb meaning "to be proud," taking the instrumental case.

replies.gloss: That makes sense, you work so hard.

replies.ru: Что именно тебе нравится в работе?
replies.gloss: What do you like about the work?

grammarFocus.construction: гордиться (imperfective present 1sg горжусь) + instrumental (своей работой)
grammarFocus.note: гордиться means 'to be proud of' and takes the instrumental. The reflexive possessive свой points back to the subject, giving the feminine instrumental своей.

variations.note: With an instrumental plural: своими детьми
A different subject and instrumental: гордимся

options.note: Using важна with для + genitive (my work matters to me)

options.ru: Мне нравится то, что я делаю.
options.note: Using нравится with то, что (I like what I do)

paraphrases.simplest: Я горжусь работой. — dropping своей is shortest.

takeaway.note: гордиться сыном (be proud of your son). One of the instrumental reflexives, with заниматься, интересоваться and пользоваться.

keyPoint: Поверь is the imperative of поверить, used as a discourse marker meaning "believe me."

grammarFocus.construction: поверить (perfective imperative поверь) + a zero-copula main clause (я всё знаю)
grammarFocus.note: Поверь works as a parenthetical imperative vouching for what follows. поверить takes the person believed in the dative (поверь мне).

variations.note: Formal or plural: поверьте
With the dative мне spelled out

options.note: Using уверять (I assure you), rather formal
Using честное слово (honestly) with в курсе

paraphrases.simplest: Поверь, я знаю. — dropping всё is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: поверить + dative (believe someone) / поверь (believe me: parenthetical imperative)
takeaway.note: Поверь мне (trust me), Не верю (I don't believe it). верить and поверить take the dative.

keyPoint: Поздравлять is imperfective, meaning "to congratulate" (pairs with поздравить).

grammarFocus.construction: прийти (perfective past plural пришли) + imperfective infinitive (поздравлять) + accusative (тебя)
grammarFocus.note: A motion verb plus an infinitive expresses purpose (пришли поздравлять = came to congratulate). The perfective поздравить often suits a single occasion better.

variations.note: With the perfective поздравить — the more natural version
A different infinitive: came to support you

options.note: With чтобы making the purpose explicit
The one-word set phrase — the shortest congratulation

paraphrases.simplest: Мы пришли тебя поздравить. — the perfective sounds more natural.

takeaway.note: Я пришёл помочь (I came to help). Motion verbs can express purpose with a bare infinitive, no чтобы needed.

keyPoint: Опоздать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "being late" (pairs with опаздывать).

grammarFocus.construction: мочь (1sg могу) + perfective infinitive (опоздать) + на + accusative (работу)
grammarFocus.note: опоздать names what you're late for with на + accusative (опоздать на работу). мочь plus an infinitive states a possibility.

variations.note: A different object: miss the train
First person plural: можем

options.note: Using задержаться (I may be held up), more measured
Using не успею (I'm afraid I won't make it)

paraphrases.simplest: Я могу опоздать. — на работу can be dropped.

takeaway.note: опоздать на урок (be late for the lesson), опоздать на самолёт (miss the plane). Always на + accusative.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Сержант is a masculine noun meaning "sergeant."

grammarFocus.construction: знать (2pl знаете) + accusative (этого сержанта, animate masculine = genitive form)
grammarFocus.note: сержант is an animate masculine noun, so its accusative matches the genitive, сержанта, and этот becomes этого.

variations.note: With a feminine noun: эту женщину
To someone you address as ты: ты знаешь

options.note: Using знаком + dative (are you acquainted with this sergeant?)
Using знакомы с + instrumental (do you know him?)

paraphrases.simplest: Вы его знаете? — a pronoun makes it shortest.

takeaway.pattern: animate masculine accusative = genitive (этого сержанта, этого человека)
takeaway.note: Inanimates keep accusative = nominative (этот документ). Animacy changing the accusative is a hallmark of Russian.

keyPoint: Невероятно is an intensifying adverb meaning "incredibly."

grammarFocus.construction: intensifier невероятно + manner adverb хорошо + петь (2pl поёте)
grammarFocus.note: невероятно means 'incredibly' and can modify another adverb or an adjective (невероятно хорошо).

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты поёшь
With удивительно (amazingly)

options.note: Using прекрасный голос (you have a beautiful voice)
Using как профессионал (you sing like a professional)

paraphrases.simplest: Вы прекрасно поёте. — one adverb says enough.

takeaway.note: An intensifier stacked on another adverb. невероятно красивый (incredibly beautiful) works the same way.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Спальня is a feminine noun meaning "bedroom."

replies.ru: Нужна ли помощь с другими комнатами?
replies.gloss: Do you need help with the other rooms?

grammarFocus.construction: убрать (perfective past plural убрали) + accusative (спальню, feminine singular accusative)
grammarFocus.note: убрать means 'to tidy, clear' and takes an accusative. спальня is feminine, giving the accusative спальню.

variations.note: A different object: did you tidy the kitchen?
To someone you address as ты: ты убрал

options.note: Using порядок (is the bedroom tidy now?)
Using the noun уборка (have you finished cleaning?)

paraphrases.simplest: Спальню убрали? — the reordered two-word version is shortest.

takeaway.pattern: убрать + accusative (tidy something) / убраться (clean up: reflexive)
takeaway.note: убрать комнату (tidy the room) versus убраться в комнате (do the cleaning in the room).

keyPoint: Злиться is an imperfective stative verb meaning "to be angry."

grammarFocus.construction: negation не + impersonal надо + imperfective infinitive (злиться) + на + accusative (меня)
grammarFocus.note: злиться means 'to be angry' and takes на + accusative. не надо plus an imperfective infinitive makes a gentle prohibition.

variations.note: A different object: don't be angry with them
As a direct imperative

options.note: Using the negated imperative of обижаться (don't take offence)
Using спокойно поговорим (let's talk calmly) — constructive

paraphrases.simplest: Не злись. — two words are enough.

takeaway.note: обижаться на + accusative (take offence at) and сердиться на + accusative (be cross with) follow the same pattern.

keyPoint: Придурок is a slang insult, a masculine noun.

replies.gloss: Why did you get so angry?

grammarFocus.construction: сказать (perfective past plural сказали) + a quoted insult («придурок»)
grammarFocus.note: придурок means 'idiot, halfwit' — colloquial and insulting, though not as strong as ублюдок. A quoted word doesn't decline.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты сказал
With дурак (fool), somewhat milder

options.note: Using назвать (did you just call me that?), calmly
Using повторите (say that again, please)

paraphrases.simplest: Что вы сказали? — lets you check without repeating the insult.

takeaway.note: All of them belittle the hearer and damage the relationship. Learn them to understand, not to use.

keyPoint: Сок is a masculine noun meaning "juice."

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть (1sg хочу) + accusative (сок, inanimate masculine = nominative form)
grammarFocus.note: The shortest way to ask for a drink. The accusative сок matches the nominative; the partitive genitive соку would mean 'some juice'.

variations.note: With the partitive genitive соку (a bit of juice)
A drink that takes the genitive: we'd like some water

options.note: Using можно + accusative — what people say in a cafe
Ordering with a dative plus пожалуйста

paraphrases.simplest: Можно сок? — two words are the natural order.

takeaway.pattern: хотеть + accusative (want a specific thing) / + genitive (want some)
takeaway.note: Я хочу воду (I want that water) versus Я хочу воды (I want some water). The case carries the quantity.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, plural accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Сюрприз is a masculine noun meaning "surprise."

replies.ru: У меня есть один для тебя.

grammarFocus.construction: любить (2pl любите) + accusative plural (сюрпризы)
grammarFocus.note: сюрприз is an inanimate masculine noun, so its accusative plural matches the nominative, сюрпризы. любить plus an accusative asks about taste.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты любишь
A different object: do you like presents?

options.note: Using нравиться with a dative, more measured
Using относиться к + dative (how do you feel about surprises?), polite

paraphrases.simplest: Вы любите сюрпризы? — already the simplest form.

takeaway.note: Я люблю сюрпризы versus Мне нравятся сюрпризы — subject and object swap places.

keyPoint: Напугать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "scaring" (pairs with пугать).

grammarFocus.construction: negation не + хотеть (perfective past хотел) + perfective infinitive (напугать) + accusative (тебя)
grammarFocus.note: напугать means 'to frighten' and takes an accusative. не хотел plus an infinitive is the standard apology: 'I didn't mean to'.

variations.note: A female speaker says не хотела
First person plural with a formal addressee

options.note: Using если напугал (sorry if I startled you)
Using не специально (I didn't do it on purpose) — the shortest

paraphrases.simplest: Не хотел тебя напугать. — dropping the subject sounds most natural.

takeaway.note: Я напугал его (I frightened him) versus Он испугался (he took fright). The -ся and the case swap the viewpoint.

keyPoint: Определённо is an adverb meaning "definitely."

grammarFocus.construction: adverb определённо + мочь (2sg можешь) + perfective infinitive (сделать) + accusative (это)
grammarFocus.note: определённо means 'definitely' and marks the speaker's confidence. мочь plus an infinitive states ability.

variations.note: To a formal or plural addressee: можете
With точно, more colloquial

options.note: Using получиться (you'll manage it) — a standard encouragement
Using не сомневаться в + prepositional (I have no doubt in you)

paraphrases.simplest: Ты справишься. — two words carry the same encouragement.

takeaway.note: All mark confidence: определённо is slightly formal, точно colloquial, безусловно bookish.

keyPoint: Покончить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "finishing with" something (pairs with кончать).

grammarFocus.construction: impersonal надо + perfective infinitive (покончить) + с + instrumental (этой работой)
grammarFocus.note: покончить means 'to put an end to' and takes с + instrumental. It sounds decisive.

variations.note: A different instrumental: end this argument

variations.ru: Нам надо покончить с этой работой.
variations.note: With the dative нам naming who must act

options.note: Using закончить + accusative, more neutral
Using пора with завершать (time to wrap it up)

paraphrases.simplest: Надо закончить эту работу. — закончить is plainer and more neutral.

takeaway.pattern: покончить с + instrumental (put an end to)
takeaway.note: покончить с прошлым (break with the past). Note the contrast with закончить + accusative (finish something).

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Обожать is a stative verb of emotion with no perfective counterpart.

replies.gloss: What exactly do you like about it?

grammarFocus.construction: обожать (imperfective present 1sg обожаю) + accusative (этот город)
grammarFocus.note: обожать means 'to adore' and is stronger than любить. It has no perfective partner.

variations.note: A different object: I adore this song
First person plural: обожаем

options.note: Using очень люблю, more measured
Using безумно нравится (I like it madly)

paraphrases.simplest: Я люблю этот город. — любить is the calmer statement.

takeaway.note: любить (like, love) < обожать (adore). обожать сладкое (adore sweet things) shows the strength of feeling.

skeleton.note: neuter noun, plural accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Показание is a neuter noun meaning "testimony."

grammarFocus.construction: читать (imperfective past plural читали) + accusative plural (показания) + genitive (героя)
grammarFocus.note: показания means 'testimony' and is normally plural. Whose testimony it is goes in the genitive (показания героя).

variations.note: A different genitive: the witness's testimony
To someone you address as ты, with a pronoun

options.note: Using знакомы с + instrumental (are you familiar with his testimony?)
Using на допросе (what did he say under questioning?), more concrete

paraphrases.simplest: Вы читали его показания? — a pronoun makes it shortest.

takeaway.pattern: показания (testimony: normally plural); possession in the genitive
takeaway.note: дать показания (give testimony), показания свидетелей (witnesses' statements). The singular показание means a meter reading.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Заслуживать is imperfective, meaning "to deserve" (pairs with заслужить).

replies.gloss: Thanks, that's really nice to hear.

grammarFocus.construction: заслуживать (imperfective present 2sg заслуживаешь) + genitive (хорошей жизни)
grammarFocus.note: заслуживать means 'to deserve' and takes the genitive (заслуживать внимания). Its perfective заслужить takes the accusative — the aspect changes the case.

variations.note: The perfective заслужить takes the accusative хорошую жизнь
Formal or plural with a different genitive: you deserve respect

options.note: Using достоин + genitive (you are worthy of), rather literary
Using иметь право на + accusative (you have a right to happiness)

paraphrases.simplest: Ты заслуживаешь лучшего. — лучшего sums it up neatly.

takeaway.note: A rare verb whose government shifts with aspect: заслуживать доверия (deserve trust) versus заслужить доверие (earn trust).

keyPoint: Ад is a masculine noun meaning "hell."

grammarFocus.construction: говорить (2pl говорите) + что clause + nominative (работа) + dash + predicate noun (ад)
grammarFocus.note: When both subject and predicate are nouns, Russian joins them with a dash (работа — ад). ад means 'hell', used figuratively here.

variations.note: With рай (heaven)
To someone you address as ты: ты говоришь

options.note: Using тяжело + dative (is work really that hard for you?)
Using изматывать (does work wear you out that much?)

paraphrases.simplest: Работа — это ад? — inserting это works just as well.

takeaway.note: Москва — столица России. With pronoun subjects the dash is usually dropped (Он врач), but between nouns it is the rule.

keyPoint: Испортить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "ruining" (pairs with портить).

grammarFocus.construction: мочь (2sg можешь) + perfective infinitive (испортить) + accusative (всё)
grammarFocus.note: испортить means 'to spoil, ruin' and takes an accusative. мочь plus a perfective infinitive expresses the risk of something happening.

variations.note: To a formal or plural addressee: можете
A different object: you could spoil the evening

options.note: Adding так for a firmer statement
Using осторожно with a negated imperative as a warning

paraphrases.simplest: Ты всё испортишь. — the plain future is shortest.

takeaway.note: Он испортил праздник (he spoiled the party) versus Молоко испортилось (the milk went off).

keyPoint: Плевать is imperfective, meaning "to spit" (pairs with плюнуть).

grammarFocus.construction: уметь (2pl умеете) + imperfective infinitive (плевать) + adverb далеко
grammarFocus.note: уметь expresses an acquired skill and takes an imperfective infinitive. плевать literally means 'to spit'; with на + accusative it means 'not to care'.

variations.note: To someone you address as ты: ты умеешь
A different infinitive: can you whistle?

options.note: Using the perfective плюнуть with a question word to ask the distance
Using кто дальше (want to bet who goes further?)

paraphrases.simplest: Вы умеете плевать далеко? — already the simplest form.

takeaway.pattern: плевать (spit) / плевать на + accusative (not care: colloquial)
takeaway.note: Мне плевать на это (I couldn't care less) is coarse. In the literal sense: Не плюй на пол (don't spit on the floor).

keyPoint: Чертовый is a slang curse-word modifier, from чёрт (devil).

grammarFocus.construction: видеть (perfective past plural видели) + accusative (этот чертовый документ)
grammarFocus.note: чертовый means 'damned' and is a mild oath derived from чёрт (devil). The spelling чёртовый also occurs.

variations.note: Without the oath — usable anywhere
With a feminine noun: чертовую бумагу

options.note: Asking directly with где — the most practical version
Using подеваться (where has it got to?), colloquial

paraphrases.simplest: Вы видели этот документ? — dropping the oath is the safe choice.

takeaway.note: Both mark irritation and belong to speech. Avoid them in formal settings; learn the чёрт family to understand it.

keyPoint: Величество is a neuter noun used as the honorific "Majesty."

grammarFocus.construction: term of address (величество) + всё as the object of понимать
grammarFocus.note: Ваше величество is "Your Majesty" and is grammatically a neuter noun phrase, so the possessive is Ваше, not Ваш. As a form of address it is cut off from the sentence by a comma. всё is the neuter pronoun "everything", here the direct object of понимать (accusative = nominative in form).

variations.ru: Ваше величество, я всё прекрасно понимаю.
variations.note: прекрасно strengthens it to "I understand perfectly well".
Moving всё to the end puts the emphasis on "everything" — word order shifts the focus.
The title changes with the addressee's rank; светлость is used for a duke.

options.note: The perfective понял reports the act of understanding as completed: "I have understood."
Dative + ясно, an impersonal construction: "everything is clear to me" — more detached than понимать.

paraphrases.simplest: Я всё понимаю.

takeaway.pattern: form of address + comma + the sentence proper
takeaway.note: Russian always separates a vocative with a comma. Titles like Ваше величество / Ваше высочество are neuter, so the agreeing possessive is neuter too (Ваше, never Ваш).

skeleton.note: feminine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Улика is a feminine noun meaning "clue, evidence."

grammarFocus.construction: perfective past заметили + accusative улику, as a question
grammarFocus.note: A question without a question word keeps statement word order and is marked only by intonation. улика (piece of evidence) is feminine, accusative улику. The perfective заметить presents noticing as a single completed event.

variations.note: эту narrows it to "this particular piece of evidence".
A negated question is the standard polite way to ask "didn't you notice...?"
With ты the past tense becomes заметил for a male addressee — it agrees with the person's gender.

options.note: обратить внимание на + accusative, "to pay attention to" — a fixed, slightly formal phrase.
Fronting the object topicalises it: "the evidence — did you see it?"

paraphrases.simplest: Вы видели улику?

takeaway.pattern: yes/no question = same word order + rising intonation
takeaway.note: There is no auxiliary inversion as in English. In writing only the question mark marks it, so when speaking, raise the pitch on the word you are actually asking about.

keyPoint: Выбраться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "getting out" with effort (pairs with выбираться).

grammarFocus.construction: мочь + perfective infinitive выбраться + из + genitive
grammarFocus.note: можем is "we can", first person plural. выбраться (to get out, with effort) governs из + genitive, and дома is the genitive of дом. The prefix вы- means "out", and -ся makes the subject move itself.

variations.ru: Мы можем выбраться из этого дома.
variations.note: этого specifies "out of this house".
The perfective сможем makes it a future prospect: "we will manage to get out".
наружу (outside) is an adverb, so it needs no preposition and no case.

options.note: Dative + удастся, impersonal: "we will succeed in getting out".

options.ru: Мы в состоянии выбраться из дома.
options.note: в состоянии + infinitive is a formal way of saying "we are capable of".

paraphrases.simplest: Мы можем выйти из дома.

takeaway.pattern: из + genitive = out of the inside of something
takeaway.note: Whatever preposition takes you in takes a matching one to get you out: в дом → из дома, на работу → с работы. Learn the pair together.

keyPoint: Хм is a thinking-pause interjection.

grammarFocus.construction: сказали + a quoted interjection «хм»
grammarFocus.note: Russian uses guillemets «» as its standard quotation marks. The quoted material does not decline — it keeps its own form while serving as the object of сказать. хм is the interjection "hmm".

variations.note: The base form: quoting the interjection back to check it.
Replacing the quote with что-то (something) checks without naming the content.
Это вы... asks who said it: "was it you who said 'hmm'?"

options.note: произнести is "to utter", focusing on the sound actually produced.
хмыкнуть is a dedicated verb for making that sound, so no quotation is needed.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы сказали «хм»?

takeaway.pattern: quotations go inside «» and never change form
takeaway.note: A quoted word is outside the case government of the sentence. «» is the normal Russian quotation mark; "..." is avoided in careful writing.

keyPoint: Забирать is imperfective, meaning "to pick someone up" (pairs with забрать).

replies.gloss: What time do you finish work?

grammarFocus.construction: future of быть (буду) + imperfective infinitive забирать
grammarFocus.note: Russian builds the future two ways: imperfective = буду + infinitive, perfective = the conjugated form itself. буду забирать means "I'll be picking you up (regularly)". после + genitive работы is "after work".

variations.ru: Я буду забирать тебя после работы каждый день.
variations.note: каждый день makes the repetition explicit — a natural fit for the imperfective.
The perfective заберу means one single pickup, today.

variations.ru: Я буду забирать вас после работы.
variations.note: вас is polite, or addresses more than one person.

options.ru: Я буду встречать тебя после работы.
options.note: встречать is "to meet" someone — not necessarily driving them home.

options.ru: После работы я буду тебя подвозить.
options.note: подвозить specifies giving a lift by car.

paraphrases.simplest: Я заберу тебя после работы.

takeaway.pattern: буду + imperfective infinitive = repeated/ongoing future; conjugated perfective = one-off future
takeaway.note: буду can never take a perfective infinitive (×буду забрать). Check the aspect of the verb before you build its future.

keyPoint: Беспокоить is imperfective, meaning "to bother/trouble" (pairs with побеспокоить).

grammarFocus.construction: subject-dropped не хочу + accusative тебя + perfective infinitive беспокоить
grammarFocus.note: The ending of хочу already shows the subject, so dropping я sounds natural. беспокоить (to trouble someone) takes the accusative, and не goes before хотеть, not before the infinitive.

variations.note: вас is the polite form — the standard opener for a visit or a phone call.
The conditional хотел бы softens it further: "I wouldn't want to trouble you".

variations.ru: Я не хочу тебя беспокоить, но это важно.
variations.note: Continuing with но turns it into the classic preamble before a request.

options.note: мешать takes the dative (тебе) and means getting in the way of what someone is doing.
Using the noun беспокойство gives the fixed apology "sorry for the trouble".

paraphrases.simplest: Не хочу тебя беспокоить.

takeaway.note: Close meanings, different government. беспокоить кого (to trouble a person), мешать кому (to be in a person's way) — the case has to be learnt verb by verb.

keyPoint: Стоп is a commanding interjection borrowed from English, meaning "stop."

grammarFocus.construction: interjection Стоп + the obligatory double negative ничего не понимаю
grammarFocus.note: Russian requires both the negative word (ничего) and не. ничего is the genitive form used for negation, because an object under negation goes into the genitive.

variations.ru: Стоп, я совсем ничего не понимаю.
variations.note: совсем intensifies it to "absolutely nothing".
Подождите (wait a moment) is politer than Стоп.

variations.ru: Стоп, я вообще ничего не понял.
variations.note: The perfective не понял limits it to what was just said: "I didn't catch any of that".

options.note: Dative + не ясно, impersonal: "nothing is clear to me".
не могу понять implies trying and failing to work it out.

paraphrases.simplest: Я ничего не понимаю.

takeaway.pattern: ничего / никто / никогда always come with не
takeaway.note: Unlike English "I understand nothing", one negative word is not enough: ничего не понимаю is correct, ×ничего понимаю is not Russian.

keyPoint: Сметь is an imperfective modal verb meaning "to dare" (pairs with посметь).

replies.gloss: Why does that bother you so much?

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative Не смей + infinitive говорить
grammarFocus.note: смей is the imperative of сметь (to dare). Не смей + infinitive is a forceful prohibition: "don't you dare". The imperfective говорить makes it "don't talk like that (any more)".

variations.note: Plural/polite form, for several people or a forceful but formal rebuke.

variations.ru: Не смей так со мной говорить.
variations.note: со мной (to me) makes it about how the person speaks to you. со is the variant of с used before consonant clusters.
никогда turns it into a permanent ban: "never dare say that".

options.note: The plain negative imperative — no смей, so much less forceful.
A rhetorical question reads as reproach rather than prohibition.

paraphrases.simplest: Не говори так.

takeaway.pattern: negative commands normally use the imperfective
takeaway.note: Не говори is a general prohibition; the perfective Не скажи instead warns "mind you don't let it slip". For forbidding something, choose the imperfective.

keyPoint: Переехать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "moving/relocating" (pairs with переезжать).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive переехать + в + accusative
grammarFocus.note: хотим is first person plural. Destination of movement is в + accusative (в этот город); в этом городе (prepositional) would mean "in this city" as a location. The case switches with direction vs. position.

variations.ru: Мы хотим переехать в этот город.
variations.note: The base form; этот is masculine singular accusative, identical to the nominative for an inanimate noun.

variations.ru: Мы хотели бы переехать в этот город.
variations.note: The conditional хотели бы is the more tentative "we'd like to move".

variations.ru: Мы хотим переехать в другой город.
variations.note: другой gives "to a different city"; the accusative form is unchanged.

options.ru: Мы собираемся переехать в этот город.
options.note: собираться + infinitive is "we intend to" — a plan rather than a wish.

options.ru: Мы планируем переезд в этот город.
options.note: Using the noun переезд makes it bookish and businesslike.

paraphrases.simplest: Мы хотим жить в этом городе.

takeaway.pattern: в + accusative = direction; в + prepositional = location
takeaway.note: переехать в город (move to the city) vs. жить в городе (live in the city). Whether the verb is motion or state decides the case after the same preposition в — a core Russian opposition.

keyPoint: Медсестра is a feminine noun meaning "nurse."

grammarFocus.construction: дать + dative (person) + accusative (thing)
grammarFocus.note: дала is the feminine past of дать. Verbs of giving take the recipient in the dative (мне) and the thing in the accusative (таблетку, from feminine таблетка). The subject медсестра is feminine, hence the -ла ending.

variations.note: After the numerals 2-4 the noun goes into the genitive singular: таблетки.

variations.ru: Медсестра дала мне таблетку от головы.
variations.note: от + genitive names what the medicine is for; от головы is colloquial for "for a headache".
An impersonal construction (plural past, no subject): "I was given a pill", leaving the agent vague.

options.note: выдать is "to issue, hand out" — bureaucratic and official in tone.
Reordering foregrounds the agent: "it was the nurse who brought me the pill".

paraphrases.simplest: Медсестра дала мне таблетку.

takeaway.note: All the giving verbs follow it — дать, сказать, показать, передать. It maps directly onto English "give someone something".

keyPoint: Поесть is perfective, meaning "to have a bite to eat" (pairs with есть).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive поесть, as a question
grammarFocus.note: поесть is есть with the prefix по-, a perfective meaning "to have a bite, to get some food in". Хотите поесть? is the standard way to offer someone a meal.

variations.note: Dropping Вы is actually more natural — the -те ending already shows the polite addressee.
A negated question offers without pressing: "wouldn't you like something to eat?"
ты + хочешь for someone you are close to.

options.note: The imperfective future будете есть is what a host or waiter asks: "will you be eating?"
перекусить is "to grab a snack" — a lighter offer than a meal.

paraphrases.simplest: Хотите поесть?

takeaway.pattern: по- + verb = "a little / one portion of"
takeaway.note: поесть (eat a bit), поспать (sleep a while), почитать (read for a bit): по- is a productive prefix forming a bounded, limited completion.

keyPoint: Месье is an indeclinable honorific from French monsieur.

grammarFocus.construction: Вы знаете, что значит + quoted word — an embedded question
grammarFocus.note: что значит «...» is an embedded question, "what does ... mean". The main clause and the subordinate clause must be separated by a comma. The quoted loanword «месье» (monsieur) does not decline.

variations.note: The base form; putting the quotation after значит is the standard order.
что такое + noun is the set way to ask for a definition: "what is a ...?"

variations.ru: Ты знаешь, что значит это слово?
variations.note: With это слово you can ask the same thing without quoting anything.

options.note: Dative + известно, impersonal, with the noun значение — distinctly formal written style.
Dropping the preamble asks directly; означает is more neutral and slightly more formal than значит.

paraphrases.simplest: Что значит «месье»?

takeaway.pattern: main clause + comma + subordinate clause (что / который / если)
takeaway.note: The comma before a subordinating conjunction is obligatory in Russian. Writing Вы знаете что... with no comma, as English often allows, is an error.

keyPoint: Присоединиться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "joining" (pairs with присоединяться).

grammarFocus.construction: Можно + perfective infinitive присоединиться + к + dative
grammarFocus.note: можно is an impersonal predicate with no subject, used to ask permission. присоединиться (to join) governs к + dative, so к вам is "to you (pl.)".

variations.note: The order can be swapped with no change of meaning; fronting к вам sounds colloquial and natural.
Adding the dative мне makes the subject explicit: "may I join you?"
могу is literally about ability, but it is also used to ask permission in practice.

options.ru: Вы не против, если я присоединюсь?
options.note: Вы не против, если... is the polite set formula "do you mind if...?"
сесть с вами (may I sit with you) is the concrete version for joining people at a table.

paraphrases.simplest: Можно к вам?

takeaway.note: "To join" requires к; ×присоединиться вас is impossible. к only ever takes the dative, so the pronouns follow suit: к нам, к тебе, к ним.

keyPoint: Госпожа is a feminine noun used as an honorific for women.

grammarFocus.construction: address Госпожа + a zero-copula nominal sentence, это ваш документ
grammarFocus.note: Present-tense "to be" is simply not expressed (zero copula): это ваш документ = "this is your document". ваш is a possessive adjective agreeing with документ (masculine singular nominative).

variations.note: The base form; Госпожа on its own sounds somewhat theatrical.
In real use the title comes with the surname: Госпожа + surname is the norm.
With the plural документы, ваши agrees in the plural — referring to a set of papers.

options.note: The negated question is the tentative "this isn't yours, is it?"
Reordering asks only about ownership — a very common short colloquial form.

paraphrases.simplest: Это ваш документ?

takeaway.note: Это ваш документ has no verb at all. The past takes Это был ваш документ and the future Это будет ваш документ — only the present goes to zero.

keyPoint: Заказать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "ordering" (pairs with заказывать).

replies.gloss: Where do you need to go?

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive заказать + accusative такси
grammarFocus.note: заказать (to order) takes the accusative. такси is an indeclinable loanword, so nominative and accusative look the same. Хочу заказать такси is the standard way to say you want a taxi.

variations.ru: Я хочу заказать такси на восемь.
variations.note: на + accusative gives the time: "order a taxi for eight o'clock".
The conditional хотел бы is the polite form for a hotel or service desk.
Dative + нужно, impersonal: "I need to order a taxi" — necessity rather than desire.

options.note: вызвать такси is the set phrase "call a taxi", here as a direct imperative request.
можно turns it into "could I order a taxi?", asking whether it is possible.

paraphrases.simplest: Я хочу заказать такси.

takeaway.note: Borrowed neuter nouns never change form, even after a preposition (в такси, на метро, в кафе). Their case is shown by position and the preposition, not by an ending.

keyPoint: Ого is an interjection of surprise.

grammarFocus.construction: сказали + the quoted interjection «ого»
grammarFocus.note: ого is a native interjection of surprise, roughly "oh!" or "wow". Material inside «» does not decline; it simply serves as the object of сказать. With Вы the past tense takes the plural form сказали.

variations.note: The base form: checking the word the other person let slip.
сейчас pins it to what was just said: "you just said 'ого', didn't you?"
Fronting почему turns it into a question about the reason.

options.note: удивиться takes the dative (чему-то): "were you surprised at something?"
Accusative Вас + удивило reverses the roles: "did that surprise you?"

paraphrases.simplest: Вы сказали «ого»?

takeaway.pattern: interjections have no gender, number or case
takeaway.note: ого, ой, ух, ай exist in one form only. In a sentence they are either quoted or set off by a comma at the start (Ого, как красиво!).

skeleton.note: 2nd person plural present, the target word

keyPoint: Волновать is imperfective, meaning "to worry someone" (pairs with взволновать).

grammarFocus.construction: волновать + accusative (to stir someone up)
grammarFocus.note: волновать is transitive — "to worry, to move someone" — and takes the accusative; меня is the accusative of я. When you are the one worrying, you use the reflexive волноваться (Я волнуюсь), so -ся flips who is affected.

variations.note: Putting меня before the verb is the natural order; Russian pronoun objects gravitate to preverbal position.
очень intensifies it: "you worry me a great deal".
With a thing as subject (ваше здоровье): "your health worries me" = I'm concerned about it.

options.note: The reflexive волноваться за + accusative means "to worry about someone", with the speaker as subject.
беспокоить also takes the accusative but leans towards "you're bothering me" rather than emotional concern.

paraphrases.simplest: Я за вас волнуюсь.

takeaway.note: Adding -ся removes the object and turns the action back on the subject. радовать/радоваться and удивлять/удивляться work the same way — the basic pattern for verbs of emotion.

keyPoint: Ха is an interjection of laughter or sarcasm.

grammarFocus.construction: сказали + the quoted laughter sound «ха»
grammarFocus.note: ха renders laughter and is often doubled as ха-ха. Quoted material stays unchanged. сказали is the plural past agreeing with Вы — the polite Вы takes plural verbs even for one person.

variations.note: The doubled form is how actual laughter is written, joined by a hyphen.
Replacing the quote with это asks whether it was meant seriously.
With ты the verb agrees in gender: сказал for a man, сказала for a woman.

options.note: засмеяться, with the prefix за-, is the perfective "to burst out laughing".
Dative + смешно, impersonal: "do you find it funny?"

paraphrases.simplest: Вы сказали «ха»?

takeaway.pattern: Вы always takes a plural verb
takeaway.note: Even when polite Вы refers to one person, the verb is plural (сказали, знаете). But predicate adjectives and nouns can stay singular — Вы правы is plural, Вы молодец is singular.

keyPoint: Расстроить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "upsetting" someone (pairs with расстраивать).

grammarFocus.construction: не хотел + perfective infinitive расстроить + accusative
grammarFocus.note: A denial of past intention: "I didn't mean to". не attaches to хотел. расстроить (to upset) is perfective and takes the accusative тебя — the perfective is right here because a single resulting state is meant. хотел shows a male speaker.

variations.note: A female speaker says хотела — the past agrees with the subject's gender.
вас is polite, or addresses several people.
The imperfective расстраивать shifts it towards "I didn't mean to be upsetting you" — the process rather than the result.

options.note: Negating специально (on purpose) makes the lack of intent explicit.
если + past gives a conditional apology: "sorry if I upset you".

paraphrases.simplest: Я не хотел тебя расстроить.

takeaway.pattern: не goes immediately before what is being negated
takeaway.note: Я не хотел расстроить (I didn't intend to upset you) and Я хотел не расстроить (I wanted to avoid upsetting you) mean different things. The position of не decides the meaning.

keyPoint: Нанять is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "hiring" (pairs with нанимать).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive нанять + animate accusative
grammarFocus.note: нанять (to hire) takes the accusative. человек is an animate masculine noun, so its accusative copies the genitive — человека — and the adjective follows suit as нового. Animate accusative = genitive is a core Russian rule.

variations.note: сотрудник (employee) fits a workplace context better; the accusative is likewise сотрудника.
двух (genitive of "two") + человек — this noun takes a special form after numerals, an exception worth noting.
The accusative of the pronoun он is его, again identical to the genitive.

options.note: взять на работу is the colloquial "to take someone on"; собираться adds "we intend to".
Dative + нужен + nominative; нужен agrees with сотрудник (masculine singular).

paraphrases.simplest: Мы хотим нанять нового человека.

takeaway.note: Я вижу нового человека (a person) vs. Я вижу новый дом (an inanimate thing, accusative = nominative). The adjective moves with the noun, so decide first whether the noun is animate.

keyPoint: Помешать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "hindering" (pairs with мешать).

replies.gloss: I'll try not to get in the way.
How exactly would I get in the way?

grammarFocus.construction: можешь + perfective infinitive помешать + dative мне
grammarFocus.note: помешать (to get in the way) governs the dative, hence мне. The prefixed perfective means one act of interference. можешь here works as a warning about what might happen, not just about ability.

variations.note: The base form: "you might get in my way".
The polite form, with можете.
The negated future reassures: "you won't be in my way".

options.note: отвлечь takes the accusative and means "to distract", so the pronoun becomes меня.

options.ru: Из-за тебя я могу не закончить.
options.note: из-за + genitive names the cause and states the consequence: "because of you I might not finish".

paraphrases.simplest: Ты можешь мне помешать.

takeaway.note: Verbs of hindering split by case: мешать/помешать govern the dative, while отвлекать/отвлечь and беспокоить govern the accusative. Learn them as pairs.

keyPoint: Исправить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "fixing" (pairs with исправлять).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive исправить + accusative это
grammarFocus.note: исправить (to fix, to correct) is perfective and takes the accusative. это is the neuter pronoun, identical in nominative and accusative. The perfective includes the result — fixing it successfully.

variations.note: Object before the infinitive — the more natural colloquial order.
With всё it becomes "I want to put everything right" — common in apologies.
должен + infinitive is "I have to fix this"; the form changes with gender (должен/должна).

options.note: сам (myself) stresses doing it personally; сам/сама by gender.
постараться is "I'll try to" — stopping short of a promise.

paraphrases.simplest: Я хочу это исправить.

takeaway.pattern: это is the same in nominative and accusative
takeaway.note: Это важно (nominative) and Я знаю это (accusative) look identical. It does change elsewhere — genitive этого, dative этому, prepositional об этом — so watch out once a preposition appears.

skeleton.note: future 1st person singular, the target word

keyPoint: Перезвонить is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "calling back" (pairs with перезванивать).

grammarFocus.construction: perfective future перезвоню + dative тебе + adverb завтра
grammarFocus.note: перезвонить is звонить with пере-, "to call back". Verbs of calling take the dative, hence тебе. Being perfective, the conjugated form itself is the future — no буду needed.

variations.note: вам is polite — the standard business formula.
утром (in the morning) is an adverbial instrumental, used with no preposition.
Equally grammatical; putting завтра before the verb sounds conversational.

options.note: связаться с + instrumental is "to get in touch", not necessarily by phone.
созвониться has reciprocal -ся, "let's talk on the phone tomorrow".

paraphrases.simplest: Я позвоню тебе завтра.

takeaway.note: ×звонить тебя is wrong: unlike English "call someone", Russian puts the person in the dative. пере- adds "again, redo" (перезвонить, переделать, перечитать).

keyPoint: Вау is an interjection borrowed from English "wow."

grammarFocus.construction: сказали + the borrowed interjection «вау»
grammarFocus.note: вау is a recent loan from English "wow", belonging to younger colloquial speech. It does the same job as native ого or ничего себе but still sounds foreign, so the register matters. Quoted material does not change form.

variations.note: The base form, quoting the loanword as it stands.
правда (really) adds surprise or gentle teasing.
ничего себе is the native expression of amazement and sounds more Russian than вау.

options.note: впечатлён/впечатлены is a passive participle, "are you impressed?" — fairly formal.
Dative + понравилось: "did you like it?", asking for the reaction directly.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы сказали «вау»?

takeaway.note: Of вау, окей and вот это да, the first two are recent loans and are best avoided in official writing or with older speakers. Recognise them, but reach for the native word yourself.

keyPoint: Сука is a neutral word for "female dog" but is also used as a strong insult.

grammarFocus.construction: perfective услышали + accusative слово + the quotation in apposition
grammarFocus.note: слово «сука» is an appositive structure, "the word сука", and the quoted part does not decline. услышать is the perfective of слышать, a single act of perception. The word itself is a strong insult — handled here only so you can recognise it.

variations.note: Swapping in это слово asks the same question without voicing the insult — the safer choice in real conversation.
An indirect question avoids repeating the offending word altogether.
ослышаться is "to mishear": "are you sure you didn't mishear?"

options.note: Replacing it with the superordinate оскорбление (an insult) lets you ask about the fact without naming the word.
выругаться is "to swear", pointing at the act rather than any specific word.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы слышали это слово?

takeaway.pattern: сука is a strong insult — for recognition only
takeaway.note: Literally "bitch (female dog)", it is extremely aggressive when aimed at a person and can even be penalised in public settings. Understand it when you hear it, but never use it; neutral substitutes are оскорбление or ругаться.

skeleton.note: indeclinable neuter noun, the target word

keyPoint: Видео is an indeclinable neuter noun.

grammarFocus.construction: imperfective present смотрим + accusative это видео
grammarFocus.note: смотрим means "we are watching" — the Russian present does not separate progressive from habitual. видео is an indeclinable neuter loanword, and это is its neuter form; the accusative looks no different.

variations.note: The base form, readable either as in progress or as a habit (watching it in every lesson).
The perfective посмотрим makes it a future: "we'll watch it through".

variations.ru: Мы смотрим эти видео каждый день.
variations.note: видео is indeclinable, so the plural looks identical; эти is the only clue that it is plural.

options.note: просматривать is "to look through, to review" — more businesslike.
Fronting the object and adding уже topicalises it: "this video, we're already watching".

paraphrases.simplest: Мы смотрим это видео.

takeaway.pattern: with indeclinable nouns, the modifiers carry number and case
takeaway.note: видео, такси, кафе, меню never change. Only the surrounding words — это/эти, в/на — show number and case, so read the modifiers carefully.

keyPoint: Классный is a colloquial adjective meaning "cool, great."

grammarFocus.construction: perfective past выбрали + adjective agreement классное кафе
grammarFocus.note: кафе is an indeclinable neuter noun, so its modifier takes the neuter singular form классное; the accusative is identical. выбрали is the plural past of выбрать, a single completed choice. классный is colloquial for "great, cool".

variations.note: хорошее is the neutral option; классное belongs to spoken style.
уже asks about progress: "have you chosen one yet?"
With ты it is выбрал for a man, выбрала for a woman.

options.note: найти is "found", shifting the focus from choosing to discovering.
A который clause turns it into "is the cafe you chose a good one?" — asking for an assessment.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы выбрали хорошее кафе?

takeaway.note: кафе never changes form but is grammatically neuter, so the adjective is классное and the past-tense verb is было (Кафе было закрыто). Follow the dictionary gender, not the ending.

keyPoint: Женатый is an adjective describing a man as married.

grammarFocus.construction: a zero-copula nominal question, Вы женатый мужчина?
grammarFocus.note: No verb expresses "are" in the present. женатый (married) is used of men and agrees with мужчина — masculine despite its -а ending — so it is masculine singular. Of a woman you say замужем, an adverb.

variations.note: The short-form predicate женаты is in fact the usual way to ask; plural to match Вы.
With ты, the short singular женат — the standard conversational form.
The form for a woman; замужем is an adverb and never changes.

options.note: The у + genitive + есть possessive construction: "do you have a wife?"
в браке (in a marriage) is the wording of documents and officialese.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы женаты?

takeaway.pattern: married = женат for a man, замужем for a woman
takeaway.note: The roots are "having a wife" (жена) and "behind a husband" (за мужем). Gender changes even the part of speech — short adjective vs. adverb — so learn the two together.

keyPoint: Оу is an interjection borrowed from English "oh."

grammarFocus.construction: interjection Оу + perfective past понял + accusative всё
grammarFocus.note: Оу is a colloquial interjection from English "oh", set off by a comma at the start. понял is perfective: understanding achieved, as a single fact. всё is the neuter pronoun in the accusative, and понял shows a male speaker.

variations.note: A female speaker says поняла — past-tense gender agreement.
А is the native interjection of dawning realisation and sounds more Russian than Оу.
теперь (now) makes it explicit that the understanding has just arrived.

options.note: Dative + ясно, impersonal: "now everything is clear to me".
Всё used on its own as an interjection adds "enough, I've got it" — closing the topic.

paraphrases.simplest: А, я всё понял.

takeaway.pattern: понимаю (I understand, state) vs. понял (I've got it, event)
takeaway.note: The imperfective present is a state; the perfective past is the moment comprehension landed. In speech Понял! is the set "got it!", while Понимаю leans towards sympathetic "I see where you're coming from".

keyPoint: Глупо is an impersonal predicate meaning "it's foolish."

replies.ru: Не совсем, у меня другое мнение.
replies.gloss: Not exactly, I have a different opinion.

grammarFocus.construction: Вы думаете, что + the zero-copula predicate adverb это глупо
grammarFocus.note: A что clause after думать is obligatorily preceded by a comma. глупо is the short neuter form working as a predicate adverb, with это as subject: "that is stupid". The long form глупое would modify a noun instead.

variations.note: The base form, asking for the other person's assessment.
считать is "to consider" — more clearly a judgement than думать.
казаться takes the instrumental, hence глупым: "does it seem stupid to you?"

options.note: по-вашему (in your view) is a parenthetical and is set off by a comma.
The noun глупость in the instrumental глупостью: "does this strike you as foolishness?"

paraphrases.simplest: Это глупо, по-вашему?

takeaway.pattern: это + a predicate adverb in -о = the standard evaluation
takeaway.note: Это глупо / интересно / важно / нормально all use the short neuter form directly as the predicate. Switch to the long form only when modifying a noun (глупая идея).

keyPoint: Отпечаток is a masculine noun meaning "imprint, mark."

replies.gloss: Is that important for the investigation?

grammarFocus.construction: perfective past оставили + accusative отпечаток
grammarFocus.note: оставить (to leave behind) is perfective and takes the accusative — a single result, "you left one". отпечаток (fingerprint, imprint) is masculine inanimate, so its accusative matches the nominative. With Вы the past is plural, оставили.

variations.note: Fingerprints normally come in the plural, отпечатки — the natural choice in real speech.
здесь narrows it down to this place; being an adverb it takes no case.
Under negation the object goes into the genitive: отпечатков. The negated question checks: "you didn't leave any, did you?"

options.note: The reflexive остаться makes the prints the subject: "are your prints still there?"
трогать + accusative, "did you touch it with your hands?" — asking about prints indirectly.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы оставили отпечаток?

takeaway.pattern: an object under negation shifts from accusative to genitive
takeaway.note: Я оставил отпечаток (accusative) vs. Я не оставил отпечатка (genitive). The genitive of negation is no longer obligatory, but it is still alive for abstract or non-specific objects.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, accusative, the target word

keyPoint: Неприятность is a feminine noun meaning "trouble."

grammarFocus.construction: попасть в + accusative (to land in a bad situation)
grammarFocus.note: попасть в + accusative means to end up in a place or situation, usually unintentionally. неприятность (an unpleasant business) is feminine; its accusative keeps the -ь ending. The perfective points to the outcome — you are already in it.

variations.note: The plural неприятности sounds more natural for "got into trouble".
беда (disaster) is graver than неприятность; its accusative is беду.
With ты it is попал for a man, попала for a woman.

options.note: The у + genitive + nominative possessive: "are you in trouble?" — the most everyday wording.
случиться с + instrumental, "to happen to someone": "has something happened to you?"

paraphrases.simplest: У вас проблемы?

takeaway.pattern: попасть в + accusative = to end up inside a situation
takeaway.note: попасть в аварию (have an accident), попасть в пробку (get stuck in traffic), попасть в тюрьму (end up in prison). It names unintended arrival, and в always takes the accusative here.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, instrumental, the target word

keyPoint: Подружка is a feminine noun meaning "girlfriend/female friend."

replies.gloss: No, but I'd like to meet her.

grammarFocus.construction: знаком с + instrumental (to be acquainted)
grammarFocus.note: знакомы is a short-form adjective, plural to agree with Вы. It governs с + instrumental, so моей подружкой is the instrumental of моя подружка. No verb "to be" appears in the present — уже знакомы is the whole predicate.

variations.ru: Вы уже знакомы с моей подругой?
variations.note: подруга is the standard word; подружка is an affectionate diminutive and sounds more casual.

variations.ru: Ты уже знаком с моей подругой?
variations.note: With ты it is знаком for a man, знакома for a woman — gender and number both move.
The instrumental of она is ней, giving с ней, "with her".

options.ru: Вы уже познакомились с моей подругой?
options.note: познакомиться с + instrumental is the perfective act of getting acquainted — the event rather than the state.
друг друга is the reciprocal pronoun in the accusative: "do you know each other?"

paraphrases.simplest: Вы знакомы с моей подругой?

takeaway.pattern: знаком с + instrumental vs. знать + accusative
takeaway.note: знать её (to know her) takes the accusative, but знаком с ней (to be acquainted with her) takes the instrumental. The first is knowledge, the second a relationship formed by introduction.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Преследовать is imperfective, meaning "to pursue/chase."

grammarFocus.construction: question word Зачем + imperfective present преследуешь + accusative меня
grammarFocus.note: зачем asks about purpose, "what for" (почему asks about cause). преследовать (to follow, to stalk) takes the accusative, and the imperfective present makes it an accusation about something still going on.

variations.note: The polite form, with преследуете.
почему asks for the reason; зачем presses harder on "to what end".
перестать + imperfective infinitive turns it into a command: "stop following me".

options.note: ходить за + instrumental is "to walk around after someone" — more everyday and concrete.
Dative + нужно + от + genitive: "what do you want from me?", confronting directly.

paraphrases.simplest: Зачем ты за мной ходишь?

takeaway.note: Зачем ты это сделал? asks what you were trying to achieve; Почему ты это сделал? asks why it happened. Mixing them up changes what you are actually demanding.

keyPoint: Ранить is biaspectual, meaning "to wound/hurt."

replies.gloss: Sorry, I didn't mean to either.

grammarFocus.construction: не хотел + infinitive ранить + accusative
grammarFocus.note: A denial of past intent. ранить (to wound) takes the accusative and is one of the biaspectual verbs — it has no separate perfective/imperfective form. It covers both physical wounds and emotional hurt. хотел shows a male speaker.

variations.note: A female speaker says хотела.
обидеть (to offend, to hurt someone's feelings) is the more usual choice in emotional contexts; it too takes the accusative.

variations.ru: Я не хотел ранить твои чувства.
variations.note: With твои чувства as the object, the figurative reading is made explicit.

options.ru: Я не хотел причинить тебе боль.
options.note: причинить боль кому, "to cause someone pain", takes the dative and sounds somewhat literary.
если + past gives the conditional apology that is actually most common in speech.

paraphrases.simplest: Я не хотел тебя обидеть.

takeaway.note: ранить has only one form and no aspect partner; context decides whether it means "is wounding" or "wounded". Others of the same kind: женить, казнить, атаковать.

keyPoint: Голодный is an adjective meaning "hungry."

replies.gloss: Let's go get something to eat.
What do you want to eat?

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the long-form adjective голодный as predicate
grammarFocus.note: Present-tense "to be" is left out. голодный is the long masculine form; colloquially it does serve as a predicate, but the norm prefers the short form голоден (Я очень голоден). очень is an intensifier for adjectives and adverbs.

variations.note: The short form голоден is the normative predicate, fitting for a temporary state.
A female speaker says голодная (long) or голодна (short), agreeing in gender.
In the plural, голодные or голодны; colloquially the long form dominates.

options.note: хотеть + the infinitive есть, "I really want to eat" — more everyday than голоден.
с голоду is a fixed genitive idiom (from с голода): "I'm starving to death", clearly hyperbolic.

paraphrases.simplest: Я хочу есть.

takeaway.pattern: short-form adjectives are the predicates of temporary states
takeaway.note: голоден, сыт, болен, занят all have the short form as their proper predicate. But some, like голодный, let the long form into predicate position in speech, so you will hear both.

keyPoint: Побрать is used only in the fixed idiom "чёрт побери" ("damn it!").

grammarFocus.construction: the mild curse Чёрт побери + accusative эту машину
grammarFocus.note: Чёрт побери! is a mild oath, roughly "damn it". побери is an archaic imperative/optative — literally "may the devil take it" — and the target stands in the accusative: эту машину from эта машина. Common in speech, but avoided in formal settings.

variations.note: The spelling with ё is correct; in practice people often write Черт with plain е.
бы + past is the optative version — more old-fashioned and theatrical.
чтоб + accusative trailing off is a colloquial, half-swallowed curse.

options.note: с + instrumental: "what is wrong with this car!" — irritation without any oath.
доконать is "to finish someone off" — colloquial, but contains no swearing.

paraphrases.simplest: Что с этой машиной!

takeaway.pattern: the чёрт family is the mildest level of swearing
takeaway.note: чёрт побери / чёрт возьми sit around English "damn" and are not part of мат (obscene language). Still, avoid them in interviews or with clients — know them for comprehension.

keyPoint: Когда-либо is a somewhat formal adverb meaning "ever."

replies.gloss: No, this is my first time.
How do you like it here?

grammarFocus.construction: the indefinite adverb когда-либо + past of быть (был) + place adverb здесь
grammarFocus.note: когда-либо means "ever, at any time" and belongs to written style; speech uses когда-нибудь. The past of быть agrees with the subject (был / была / были). Location is здесь, an adverb with no case.

variations.note: когда-нибудь is the conversational standard; когда-либо suits documents and legal texts.
была for a woman; раньше (before) makes it sound naturally colloquial.
With вы the past is always plural были; word order is free.

options.note: бывать is the iterative imperfective "to visit (repeatedly)" — close to "have you been here before?"
Using впервые (for the first time) asks the same thing from the opposite side, as a statement question.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты когда-нибудь был здесь?

takeaway.note: кто-нибудь (anyone at all), кто-либо (any party whatsoever — formal), кто-то (someone definite but unidentified). For conversation, master the -нибудь vs. -то contrast.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, instrumental, the target word

keyPoint: Шлюха is an extremely strong insult, a feminine noun.

replies.gloss: I didn't mean to offend anyone.

grammarFocus.construction: negative imperative Не называй + accusative её + instrumental шлюхой
grammarFocus.note: называть кого кем, "to call someone something", puts the name in the instrumental (шлюха → шлюхой). Negative imperatives use the imperfective, hence называй. шлюха is a severely insulting word for a woman — treated here only so that you recognise it.

variations.note: так (like that) says exactly the same thing without voicing the insult — the version to use in practice.
Adding Не смей makes it an emphatic prohibition: "don't you dare call her that".
оскорблять (to insult) takes the accusative and stops the behaviour in neutral terms.

options.note: перестать + imperfective infinitive, "stop insulting her", with no slur involved.
нельзя + infinitive, impersonal, with о + prepositional: "you can't talk about her like that".

paraphrases.simplest: Не называй её так.

takeaway.pattern: шлюха is a slur — recognise it, never say it
takeaway.note: It is a very aggressive attack on a woman and can expose you to an insult charge. The grammar worth taking away is называть кого (accusative) кем (instrumental); practise it with так or это слово instead.

keyPoint: Сражаться is imperfective, meaning "to fight."

grammarFocus.construction: imperfective future будем сражаться + adverb вместе
grammarFocus.note: сражаться (to fight, to do battle) is reflexive and has no perfective partner, so its only future is будем + infinitive. The opponent goes in с + instrumental. вместе is an adverb and never changes.

variations.ru: Мы будем сражаться вместе до конца.
variations.note: до конца (to the end) is до + genitive.

variations.ru: Мы будем сражаться с ними вместе.
variations.note: с + instrumental (с ними) names the enemy explicitly.
бороться is "to struggle" and works for abstract fights too (бороться за права).

options.note: воевать means "to wage war" and is restricted to military contexts.
Figuratively, "we'll go all the way together" — no fighting named directly.

paraphrases.simplest: Мы будем бороться вместе.

takeaway.pattern: verbs with no perfective have only the буду + infinitive future
takeaway.note: сражаться, работать, жить and other state or process verbs form their future just one way. Conversely, with a perfective verb буду + infinitive is forbidden.

keyPoint: Извиниться is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "apologizing" (pairs with извиняться).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive извиниться
grammarFocus.note: извиниться (to apologise) is reflexive; the person you apologise to takes перед + instrumental (перед тобой) and the reason за + accusative (за опоздание). Хочу извиниться is the standard way to open an apology.

variations.note: перед + instrumental names the addressee; ×извиниться тебя is impossible.
за + accusative names the reason: "I want to apologise for being late".
The conditional хотел бы is a notch more formal — used in official apologies.

options.note: просить прощения (to beg forgiveness) takes the genitive and is a somewhat formal, polite set phrase.
The imperative извини + accusative меня — the most everyday "I'm sorry".

paraphrases.simplest: Я хочу извиниться.

takeaway.note: The person takes перед + instrumental, the reason за + accusative. Get the prepositions wrong and the apology fails, so learn the whole frame together.

skeleton.note: 1st person plural present, the target word

keyPoint: Видеться is imperfective, meaning "to see each other" (pairs with увидеться).

grammarFocus.construction: reciprocal -ся in видимся + frequency adverb часто
grammarFocus.note: видеться is видеть plus -ся, a reciprocal verb meaning "to see each other". Its subject must be plural (мы, они) or else it needs с + instrumental. часто (often) sits naturally with the imperfective present.

variations.note: Same meaning with a different order; putting здесь before the verb sounds conversational.
редко (rarely) reverses the frequency.

variations.ru: Я часто вижусь с ним здесь.
variations.note: With a singular subject the partner appears as с + instrumental — obligatory for reciprocal verbs.

options.note: встречаться is also reciprocal; note it can mean both "meet" and "be dating", so context matters.
Dropping -ся and taking an accusative gives the one-way "I often see you here".

paraphrases.simplest: Мы часто здесь видимся.

takeaway.pattern: reciprocal -ся needs a plural subject or с + instrumental
takeaway.note: видеться, встречаться, обниматься, целоваться, созвониться all mean "each other". With a singular subject you must add с кем (Я вижусь с ним).

keyPoint: Вкусный is an adjective meaning "tasty."

grammarFocus.construction: любить + accusative + adjective agreement вкусный кофе
grammarFocus.note: кофе is an indeclinable loanword and is traditionally masculine, hence вкусный кофе. Colloquially you also hear the neuter (вкусное кофе), but the norm is masculine. любить + accusative expresses liking.

variations.note: хороший is the neutral option; вкусный focuses on the taste.
чай is an ordinary masculine noun and does decline (вкусного чая, etc.).
With ты, любишь — only the verb ending changes.

options.note: Dative + нравится: the thing liked becomes the subject, so кофе is nominative here.
разбираться в + prepositional, "to know a lot about" — shifting from taste to expertise.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы любите кофе?

takeaway.note: The form never changes, but the gender is masculine, so adjectives and past tenses are masculine too (вкусный кофе, кофе остыл). The neuter is colloquial drift; exams expect masculine.

keyPoint: Беременный is an adjective meaning "pregnant," used only for women.

grammarFocus.construction: zero copula + the short-form adjective беременна
grammarFocus.note: No present-tense "to be". беременна is the short feminine form of беременная and exists only as a predicate. сейчас (now) is an adverb. Short forms describe temporary states; long forms describe permanent qualities and modify nouns.

variations.note: Dropping сейчас changes nothing: the short form alone conveys the temporary state.
The past adds была + the short form, agreeing in gender and number.
The long form беременная modifies the noun женщина; normatively it is not used as a predicate.

options.note: ждать + accusative (ребёнка, animate so genitive-shaped): "she is expecting a baby" — the euphemism.
у + genitive + будет + nominative: "she is going to have a baby" — the most neutral phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Она беременна.

takeaway.pattern: short adjective = predicate, long adjective = modifier
takeaway.note: Она больна (she is ill right now) vs. Она больная женщина (she is a sickly woman). The short form states a temporary condition, and it survives in common words like беременна, больна, занята, свободна.

skeleton.note: feminine noun, plural genitive, the target word

keyPoint: Миля is a feminine noun meaning "mile."

grammarFocus.construction: сколько + genitive plural миль, in an embedded question
grammarFocus.note: сколько asks about quantity and always puts the following noun in the genitive. миля (mile) is feminine, and its genitive plural is миль — a zero-ending form. The main clause Вы знаете is separated by a comma.

variations.note: Russia uses километр, not miles; the genitive plural is километров.
The direct question, with the preamble dropped.

variations.ru: Вы знаете, сколько это в милях?
variations.note: в + prepositional plural милях is "in miles" — the way to ask for a unit conversion.

options.note: Using the noun расстояние (distance) gives a more formal wording.
The predicate adverb далеко gives the most colloquial version: "is it still far?"

paraphrases.simplest: Сколько здесь километров?

takeaway.note: сколько книг / сколько людей / сколько миль. It governs like the numerals from five up; only 2-4 take the genitive singular (две мили). Quantity expressions work in these three tiers.

keyPoint: Угадать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of "guessing correctly" (pairs with угадывать).

grammarFocus.construction: можешь + perfective infinitive угадать + accusative ответ
grammarFocus.note: угадать (to guess right) is perfective and takes the accusative — it includes the successful outcome. ответ is masculine inanimate, so its accusative matches the nominative. можешь + infinitive asks whether you can.

variations.note: The base form — standard when posing a riddle.
The polite form, with можете.
попробовать + infinitive: "try to guess", recast as a command.

options.note: догадываться means working it out by inference, focusing on the process.
Как ты думаешь is a parenthetical opener set off by a comma: "what do you reckon?"

paraphrases.simplest: Ты можешь угадать ответ?

takeaway.note: The perfective угадать contains the hit; the imperfective гадать is the guessing around. Hence Не гадай, а спроси — "don't speculate, just ask" — negates the process with the imperfective.

skeleton.note: 2nd person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Прятаться is imperfective, meaning "to hide" (pairs with спрятаться).

replies.gloss: I just want to be alone.

grammarFocus.construction: Зачем + the reflexive verb прячешься + place adverb здесь
grammarFocus.note: прятаться (to hide) is прятать (to hide something) plus -ся, so the subject hides himself. зачем asks about purpose. The present прячешься means the hiding is still going on.

variations.note: With вы, прячетесь; the word order can be shuffled freely.
от + genitive asks who you are hiding from — the typical complement of прятаться.
почему asks for the reason; зачем asks for the intention.

options.ru: Что ты здесь делаешь в укрытии?
options.note: в укрытии (in hiding) uses в + prepositional, naming the state with a noun.
A recast as a summons; выходи is the imperative of выходить.

paraphrases.simplest: Зачем ты здесь прячешься?

takeaway.pattern: прятать что vs. прятаться (to hide oneself)
takeaway.note: Adding -ся removes the object: Я прячу деньги (I hide the money) vs. Я прячусь (I hide). мыть/мыться and одевать/одеваться work the same way.

skeleton.note: 1st person singular present, the target word

keyPoint: Ценить is a stative imperfective verb meaning "to value/appreciate."

replies.ru: Это самое малое, что я могу сделать.
replies.gloss: It's the least I can do.

grammarFocus.construction: imperfective present ценю + accusative твою помощь
grammarFocus.note: ценить (to value, to appreciate) takes the accusative. помощь is a feminine noun in -ь, and its accusative stays помощь. The possessive твою is feminine singular accusative. The present states how you feel right now.

variations.note: очень strengthens the gratitude.
вашу is the polite form; the feminine accusative ending is the same.

variations.ru: Я ценю то, что ты сделал.
variations.note: то, что + clause gives "I appreciate what you did" — the pattern for an abstract object.

options.note: спасибо за + accusative is the everyday "thanks for ...".
благодарен (m) / благодарна (f) is a short form; the person goes in the dative, the reason in за + accusative.

paraphrases.simplest: Спасибо за помощь.

takeaway.pattern: feminine nouns in -ь have accusative = nominative
takeaway.note: помощь, любовь, ночь, дверь never change in the accusative. Masculine -ь nouns (день → день) also match, but their declension diverges from the genitive onwards.

keyPoint: Возражать is imperfective, meaning "to object" (pairs with возразить).

grammarFocus.construction: imperfective future не буду возражать
grammarFocus.note: возражать (to object) is imperfective, so the future is буду + infinitive, with не attached to буду. What you object to takes против + genitive, and the person you object to takes the dative. The phrase is a standard way of consenting.

variations.note: The base form: "I won't object".
The present means consenting here and now — the usual choice when granting permission.
The shortest consent, using против + genitive: "I'm not against it".

options.note: согласен (m) / согласна (f), short form: "I agree", a more active endorsement.
Prefacing with Как хочешь (as you like) hands the decision over.

paraphrases.simplest: Я не против.
